utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just deal with two preliminary matters; it will take no time at all. We move on to Major-General Pringle. And I just would like some clarification from the Court in relation to dealings with experts. In my jurisdiction, counsel can speak to experts in the middle of their testimony. I believe it may well be the practice here that that is not the case. And so really all I wish to have is clarification obviously for Prosecution and Defence that if experts are being called they either are or are not able to speak to the lawyers during their testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The position with which I am familiar in this Tribunal and elsewhere is as you understood, that they may not be spoken to. So that if something unusual arises, which you think requires such, it would require an application to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm quite happy with that. It just helps both parties. The second relates to Witness, I think it is 002, is the last civilian witness who gave evidence, and there was reference to a notebook which we have, despite many searches, not have any copies of. Apparently that witness contacted the investigation department last night and has said that he has located the document. I have arranged for the following to occur. For it to be taken to the field office in the city in which he lives, for it to be photocopied there and for the original to be sent here to The Hague and obviously my learned friends to have photocopies of that document and translations to be made of it. If that sounds wonderful, I hope, but there is a difficulty, and it is quite simply this: Your Honour may remember we had Mr. Kypr who had also a notebook, we tried to interpret it, and sometimes people use their own techniques of recording notes. My understanding is that that might well be the same problem for this witness. So I am going to see whether in actual fact it is possible for a translation to be done in the city where he is with an authorised interpreter, but nevertheless for copies to be forwarded up to this Court and the lawyers as soon as possible. So that is the modus operandi that I was going to deal with in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I must say that sounds very encouraging, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. May I call then, please, Major-General Pringle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to take the affirmation which is printed on the card handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we commence, there are copies of the report for the Chamber. They have been slightly modified. My learned friends have seen those amendments. And perhaps if those hard copies can be forwarded. They're being brought down and will be here in a moment. But may I just deal with the introduction with regard to Major-General Pringle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do we not have them already?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour may remember that there was objection taken to references to one or two witnesses. What we have done, my understanding is, and what I've been informed is, is that the copies that you have are the originals. And the modified copy is going to be in colour in certain parts. If I just assist the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's enough. You can carry on. I thought, not having opened it, that this document was the modified copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it may well be. Can I just clarify to see? It may well be that parties have been more efficient than has otherwise been the case. If one goes to page 13 where it is the topic -- it says "Command climate."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have trouble finding a page called 13. Oh, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have an interruption in the pagination. And then it continues. Command climate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If one looks down at the footnotes, one can see, for example, on footnote 56, that there is a reference to a man called Topola appears in other witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Brutalising prisoners of war. That is underlined in red. The red --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we then deal with the curriculum vitae of Major-General Pringle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I have your full name please?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Andrew Robert Douglas Pringle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's correct to say that you had the good fortune to serve in the British army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That you are currently a retired major-general from the army, having served there for 37 years?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That you are currently employed as a defence consultant with I perhaps can describe as a wide-ranging portfolio; for example, providing assistance on two occasions to NATO command and control studies?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal then, please, with the -- your professional background. Is it right that you entered the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst as an officer cadet in 1964; that you graduated in two years from Sandhurst; and you were commissioned in the Royal Green Jackets, one of the principal and most famous of the infantry regiments which has three battalions, I believe. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct and kind of you to put it like that, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My pleasure. Can we deal then, please, that you served as platoon commander with the battalion in Cyprus?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In Cyprus, given the nature of the work that you had to do, there was considerable tension at that time between the two ethnicities or nations, both Turkish and Greek, which in its own way created its own tension; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You then attended a three-year degree course in applied science in the Royal Military College in Shrivenham, and you subsequently rejoined your infantry battalion in 1971?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In 1971, if I deal with it in this way, you then commenced a number of tours, as it's called, of Northern Ireland, when the troubles, as they are called again, were at their peak, that involved disputes between the IRA and loyalist paramilitary -- paramilitaries, and your tours were through 1971, 1972, 1973, 1978, 1979, 1980, 1981, and 1983; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct Your Honours, but I could describe it as a counter-terrorism campaign rather than disputes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm trying to be as neutral perhaps as I can. May I then deal please with your position through Northern Ireland. You were appointed, as I say, platoon commander, you then became adjutant company second in command, company commander, concluding as an operational staff officer at headquarters in Northern Ireland; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Moving on, you attended junior staff college, it was called the junior command and staff course, 1975, and you then were selected to go to what some would describe as the prestigious command and staff course at Army Staff College, I believe based in Sandhurst, is that right, 1976 to 1977.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: At Camberley, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. The selection process involved there 30 per cent of the officers only were selected for staff training. And that was a result of a competitive examination and obviously receiving the appropriate and proper recommendations on their annual appraisal reports, and you subsequently returned to that college as a member of the directing staff between 1983 and 1985 inclusive. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, you then in relation to the Army Staff College, if I deal with it in this way, you attended the Royal Military College of Science at Shrivenham, that was a one-year course, because I believe you have an honour's degree in applied science. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The second year you concentrated on command and staff responsibilities and tactics up to divisional level, which is -- well, up to divisional level, that the course itself could be described as wide-ranging in content and there were studies in command including presentations and various other discussions with -- with persons who had first-hand knowledge. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dealing with the staff college exercise, is it right to say that there were exercises themselves which included various aspects of military observations, or I should say operations at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You then returned to command your infantry battalion, that's the 3rd Battalion of Royal Green Jackets, that was from 1985 until 1988, that was in Germany and the U.K. And it was on that occasion that you had what could be described as close contact with the German army, and you subsequently and consequently were exposed to doctrine and operating procedures. And you then went on a tour of duty to the Ministry of Defence as a colonel in the military operations branch operating at strategic level, responsible for general staff policy which was worldwide. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Following that you then attended the Royal College of Defence Studies, otherwise known as the war college, for one year. Perhaps I won't go into the detail of that, but it would be -- would it be right to say that half the members of the war college were British, drawn from military police, other government departments, and the other half were drawn from around the world and it was predominantly from the military?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Moving on in time, I think it's right to say that you had, as has been described, a tour in the cabinet office between 1992 until 1994. There you led a branch in the assessment staff working for the joint intelligence committee. In 1994, you moved to Germany where you took command of the 20th Armoured Brigade. There you were subsequently deployed with your headquarters and a number of units to Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995. On that occasion, you were commander of the UN sector southwest based in Gornji Vakuf; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dealing with your operational tour, unfortunately, I think it coincided with what could be described as the total break-down of the cease-fire, and from April 1995 you describe the conflict between the different ethnic groups as having extreme intensity until it was finally brought to an end with the signing of the Dayton Agreement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that you have described this tour, was a lesson for a commander to operate in the context of what you have described as strategic muddle and lack of clarity?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, if I may just abbreviate my questions for a moment.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: We were operating in a climate of nuclear objectives. We were sitting in the middle of a war that was raging all round us as the United Nations with very restrictive rules of engagement. We were taking directions both from the United Nations and nationally. There was an international state of disagreement as to what should or should not be done. And for the commanders on the ground their best guidance was simply to do what they thought was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it's right then that after a tour you were as director of land warfare in 1996 until 1997, you became responsible for the army concepts and doctrine, and you then returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina as the NATO commander, multi-national division southwest, again based in Banja Luka; that was from 1997 until 1998. And I think it was here that you described yourself as having considerable high-level contact with Bosnian Serb military police and civilian authorities; also contacts with a wide range of international humanitarian agencies. And then finally your final posting was Chief of Staff/director of operations at the permanent joint headquarters at Northwood in the United Kingdom, there is a slight misprint in the report, I see, 1998 until 2001. And it was there that the United Kingdom directed, deployed and sustained forces in respect of numerous operations around the world, and there you had dealings at operational interface with deployed commanders in forward theatres of operations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As I have already said, you retired from the army, I believe, in 2001?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The reports are here. In conclusion therefore, is it right to say that you have commanded troops and been involved in the chain of command in relation to countries other than the U.K., those countries and troops coming from Spain, Turkey, the Netherlands, Canada, the United States of America, the Czech Republic, New Zealand, and Malaysia, and that you have cooperated closely with headquarters and troops from Australia, France, Germany, Sweden, Norway and Finland. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct. The only thing I would add is I have had the good fortune to command at every level from platoon to division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you forgive me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just pass these forward, please. This is for the Bench. Your Honour, may I now deal with one or two matters. If Your Honour looks at page 13 again, and I will provide, I hope in the near future, coloured copies. The copies that you have will not be coloured, but the reason will become obvious in a minute. But the report is unchanged, the lining is there, but the colouring will help. We also wish to insert the exhibit number because a number of these documents have been exhibited. But if we look, for example, at page 13, footnote 56, the one I've already referred to, I hope that there is a line underneath the phrase: "Topola appears in other witness statements." As I say, what I intend to do when the printing process is up and running is for the Court to have that underlined in colour. That will be in red and will denote that it's something that we do not seek to rely upon. If one then moves to page 29 by way of example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Judge Thelin has the benefit of colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Judge Thelin is a very lucky Judge, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: So far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So far. Could well be true. But in any event, we will try and ensure that Your Honour and Your Honour's colleague will have the coloured copies as well. But if I move to page 29 and we look take, for example, footnote 124, we have got there: "See for example Witness P-202," that witness was not called. It will be underlined in red, and therefore we do not rely on that. However, if you looks across, you will see then, and it will be in blue in Judge Thelin's document, or aquamarine, Witness P-022, then it should show T and a reference, 4959, 4960. That stands T for transcript. So what we have attempted to do is to extract from transcripts evidence that is comparable to the witness statement, and we have attempted to do it that way. As I say, I will get the additional copies. But that is the way that the report has been structured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you close that page, I notice in the text, in the paragraph numbered 84 there is underlining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that indicating that that is not relied on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If one looks at, for example, footnote 126, at the very bottom, there is underlining, Judge Thelin will see it, it is in red, that relates to an officer called Tesic, who the Prosecution most certainly will not seek to rely upon. It is replaced by Witness P-030, the transcript is there. Then just below it at 127, Ibid relates to the reference from Tesic. And so consequently that was something that he had originally stated but it will be replaced by the note -- footnote 126.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So I hope that that is clear. May I then also pass forward to the Court two bundles of hard copy. These are documents ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I hope Your Honour has already got those two bundles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two heavy black folders, if that's what you mean by bundles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, two heavy black bundles. Can I just deal please with the explanation for these bundles of documents. Your Honour will see that there is reference to footnote 1 and it flows through and should link to every footnote in the -- Major-General Pringle's report. I have stuck with footnotes at this time. Many of those documents are now exhibits, and really for completeness it is better -- is there one or two? For completeness, it is better if we stick to footnotes because that's actually on the report. I will subsequently serve on the Court a further amended report from General Pringle where the footnotes will be replaced with exhibits. So when the report is available for you to consider it, you will have not only the footnote, but the exhibit which have been principally exhibited in Theunens's document, so that is the way it will be done. To assist the Court again, because it's not quite as straightforward as one would think, when we have "Ibid" referred to in the footnotes, often it will be, for example -- if we go to footnote 6. So it's the largest bundle. If one goes to footnote 6, one will find that there is nothing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm glad of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's not an omission, it's unusually deliberate, and therefore we have got on the page footnote 6 is in the range of footnote 2. So what we have tried to do is go back to the original source document. So if, for example, the Court find that there's something missing, it, I hope, will show that in actual fact there is a reference specifically back to footnote 2. On occasion, one will find a reference going back three or four times. I'm afraid there is no way out of it, because of the way the report has been written, and that's not a criticism in any way. I hope that that is clear. May I then deal, please, with the first topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: General, do you have your report in front of you, and you have got the documents in the two files; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we deal, please, with the first topic. It is quite simply this: Is there a document where you have found an apparent definition of what "command" means? And I'm going to ask the Court to look at footnote 1, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Command refers to the authority vested in an individual for the direction, coordination and control of military forces. This has a legal and constitutional status --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just before we proceed, may we make sure everybody gets that page. Unfortunately matters move rather slowly. So it's footnote 1. It relates to the Law on All People's Defence. And I would like to refer you, if I may, please, to Article 112. And the registry have got an index prepared for them to assist them on putting it on e-court. Thank you very much. So, General, would you be kind enough please to refer us to -- or read for us, please, Article 112 where you have referred to footnote 1 on your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. This represents the legal and constitutional basis, and Article 112 on the Law on All People's Defence states that: "Command in the armed forces shall be founded on the principles of unity of command with respect to the use of forces and resources, unity of authority and the obligation to implement decisions, commands and orders of a superior officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as far as you are aware, is that comparable to "command" in the -- I will call the western armies, or perhaps NATO forces, as you know it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we move on to the second point, which is footnote 2, because I'd like to ask you: Are you aware - indeed I think it's right it say, there's no dispute - that you have consulted the Federal Secretariat for National Defence command and control document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We note it as Exhibit 394. Could we please go to section 5, or should I say page 27 in the hard copy. I hope everyone has now got that. You should have before you: "Principles of command and control." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal then, please, with section 5, as I say, dealing with single authority, going across to page 28. I want to specifically refer to that. So page 28 at the bottom of footnote 2. What are the principles that apply there, please, in respect of single authority?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, this doctrine states that: "The principle of single authority in command and control implies an inalienable right of a commander to command and control a subordinate command and unit in keeping with the powers deriving from the competence ascribed to a specific level of command and control. This principle ensures that in the process of command and control there is only one superior who issues commands and to whom the others report about the execution of tasks." Do you wish me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It continues: "The commander's authority is stipulated by regulations. It is his right to make decisions for which he is therefore solely responsible. In his work, a commander relies on his aides, the staff, and other command organs. The rights and obligations of these organs are stipulated by regulations, and they are responsible for their scope of work. A commander may delegate some of his duties and obligations on the Chief of Staff, his aides, a staff organ and subordinated commands, but he cannot delegate the responsibility for the situation in the unit and its use."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with that last sentence, please. "But he did not delegate the responsibility for the situation in the unit and its use." What exactly does that mean in layman's language?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That means that the commander is ultimately responsible for everything that happens in his command and the acts and actions of those under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal then, please, with the issue of subordination. It is the following page. The subheading is on page 28, but the part that I would like to deal with in English is on page 29, and it is four lines from the top, commencing "subordination within." Would you be kind enough to read that, please, and then I will ask some questions in respect of it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: This extract reads: "Subordination within a military organisation introduces a chain of command from top to bottom - from the SFRJ Presidency to a squad. Underlying the chain of command are the duty, right and responsibility of superiors to make decisions and assign tasks, whereas subordinates have the duty, right and responsibility to carry them out accurately and in time."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just deal with the issue of subordination here. We have the commander who has the ultimate responsibility. To what extent must he be informed of the task of which he has assigned to a subordinate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: He must be fully informed, because he is accountable, and therefore he requires information to flow up and down the chain of command, such that he has a full, if you like, situational awareness of everything that is going on in his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does that mean that the subordinate therefore has no responsibility for the task assigned to him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The subordinate has absolute authority -- absolute responsibility to carry out the order assigned to him in the manner ascribed by his commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I refer to your report, please, paragraph 16. That comes under the subheading of command and control. Six lines in the English version it starts "in relation to accountability involves liability and obligation to answer to a superior." You refer here clearly to accountability and control. What do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Accountability, as I say in my report, involves a liability and obligation to answer to a superior for the proper use of delegated responsibility, authority and resources. At every level of a command chain those receiving orders are accountable to their superior officer for the way in which those orders are carried out. Control -- do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I do, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Control is the process through which a commander is assisted by his staff to organise and direct and coordinate the plethora of activities that the forces under his command are carrying out. Command and control are thus inextricably linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to move on a little, if I may. You have had the opportunity of reading the report by Major-General Zorc dated the 1st of February, 2004. And that will be found at footnote 4, for the Court's assistance, and I will refer to it in a moment. There he refers to command and control and other related issues for the JNA. The question I wish to ask is as follows: Are you able to comment or observe within your professional capacity on the similarities between the command and control system in respect of the JNA and other developed armies of which you are aware?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In his report, Major-General Zorc states that the commander control system in the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia was very similar to the system of other European armies, having developed, in the course of time, within what he describes as the continental military tradition. Now, I would agree with that. I have read many extracts and tomes from JNA doctrine, and I've been extremely impressed by its thoroughness and its similarity to the sort of doctrine that I have grown up with and an awareness of doctrines of other continental armies. We referred to the German army whilst you were running through my CV. There is an absolute similarity between the doctrine laid down by the JNA and what Major-General Zorc describes as European armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To assist the Court, may I refer, please, to footnote 4, top right-hand corner, page 3. And there is the reference, the first four lines in respect of the similarity of the European armies. And again, merely to assist the Court. Could I ask you then, please, General, to move to page 6 of the Zorc report. I will be referring to page 6 and page 10 in due course. Page 6, it is subheading "Forming an operational group/OG and its command and control level." When one looks at an operational group and its formation, do you see any similarity in relation to an operational group formation and/or its function?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Moore, I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have reference to "c), Forming an operational group."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And its command and control level?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: An operational group, if we suggest that it is created on an ad hoc basis?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question that I want to ask is: With something like an operational group creation on an ad hoc basis, what is its function?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: An operational group would be formed from a number of different formations brought temporarily together under a single commander for a specific operation, usually for a defined time. So its composition would be in accordance with the task and size of the area of responsibility it was allocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how would one deal with command and control with regard to an ad hoc creation like an operational group?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, the ad hoc part poses extra problems for the operational group commander. It's all very well commanding your own formation which you have trained and which you live with on a day-to-day basis and where you know all the personalities involved. When you start to add to that formation with different formations that you may not have experienced before, you may not have trained, and you may not even know, and when you compound that with the fact that they may be a mixture of regular forces, territorial forces, volunteer forces, the commander has a problem. And he would be aware of that. And so he would have to deal with those under his command in accordance with their level of professionalism, expertise and knowledge. And in particular, he would have to pay very careful attention to the less well-trained element, which I would define here as the territorial element and the volunteer element, which he would not expect to act in the same way as his well-trained regular forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like -- I would like to turn to page 9, top right-hand corner, please. But I want to go to g) again of Zorc's report. I want to deal with it very briefly. So it should be top right-hand corner. It should be the heading of "Monitoring conditions and the situation at higher and lower levels of command and control." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If you forgive me, General, I just want to check that the documents that have arrived are in colour. Thank you very much. You have, to a large extent, dealt with this. But in relation to the regulations themselves, is it right it say that there is actually categories indicating the -- monitoring the conditions, situation at higher and lower levels of command and control. I would like to deal with the second paragraph, commencing "in immediate combat all commanders." Would you be kind enough to read that out, please, and then we'll deal with the content.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. Major-General Zorc's reports states that: "In immediate combat all commanders should be informed of the situation two levels above (first level above in detail, second level above - approximately) and two levels below. A corps commander then makes a plan of combat activities, respecting the decisions made by the commanders of the first subordinate levels - at battalion level - on engaging their units."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What the importance of the doctrine of two up/two down?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Two up/two down will be familiar to European armies or certainly NATO armies. And it's interesting that Major-General Zorc says the same thing is applying in the JNA. By thinking two up and two down, a commander at any level puts -- is able to interpret his orders in the context two up of the much bigger picture, and therefore he understands why he is being ordered to do what he -- what he has been ordered to do. And a commander thinking two levels down ensures that a commander gives proper cognizance when allocating tasks to the resources required to carry out those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be kind enough, please, then to turn to page 10, top right-hand corner. It is i), subheading i). The title is "What must a commanding officer do to ensure that his orders are being carried out." Do you have that particular reference?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The word I wish to focus on is "ensure," "what must a commanding officers do to ensure." Now may we deal, please -- obviously I rely on the whole of the document, but I wish to focus six lines down, sentence commencing "the commanding officer himself." Do you have that reference?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to read out that sentence and then I will deal with it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: The sentence reads: "The commanding officer himself or his command staff must supervise the execution of his orders and help if and when necessary (this activity is called 'control and help')."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And finally to read one other part. If one looks at the penultimate paragraph, the second-last paragraph, it is three lines from the bottom of that paragraph, commencing "in cases when officers under their command." Do you see that reference?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to read that out, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I do that, I'll just add on the sentence to the transcript I've just read out that I omitted, because I consider it to be highly pertinent. After "this activity is called control and help" it goes on to say: "For orders of utmost importance, the commanding officer should be involved himself." Turning now to the transcript, the second one, it reads: "In cases where officers under their command are not experienced enough or if there are reserve units insufficiently trained in the task, commanding officers tend to become personally involved in controlling and helping those officers under their command."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question that I have, although in actual fact you have pretty much dealt with it, is why is it necessary for a commanding officer to become personally involved when there are matters of -- to use the words, "utmost importance."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Because as we have mentioned already, the commanding officer is responsible for everything that happens in his command and is accountable for everything that happens in his command. Therefore, if some elements of his command are less well-trained than others, he has a responsibility to ensure, nevertheless, that they understand his orders, understand how they are to be carried out, and supervises that they are being carried out in that way and were they or not to take the necessary action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I please tender this document, Zorc's report, as an exhibit. It is 65 ter number 961. But it's subsumed within the bundle that we have already provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Thank you. I think the situation here is similar to the one encountered yesterday with Professor Adinovic's [phoen] report that was used in the Kunarac case. Yesterday the Defence made a similar objection to Mr. Adinovic's report in the Kunarac case. We don't have a ruling on that yet. I'm afraid my learned friend cannot now be tendering the report of a witness who has not been heard in this case and who once testified in another case. It's all right to ask Mr. Pringle what he thinks about particular subjects from this report, but another thing is that we are not given a chance to cross-examine the author of this report in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question of the admission of the document will be dealt with at the same time as the issue raised yesterday, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Will the -- will I be permitted to submit in relation to the admissibility of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You could even do it now, if you wish, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't want to use the time, but I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you run entirely out of time, written submissions within a day or two next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because the decision will be coming next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And in the meantime, it will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With the reference number 599, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I, General, please, refer to paragraph 18 of your report. With regard to this paragraph your report returns to really footnote 2, the text-book in respect of command and control. Dealing with it briefly, there is reference in your report to the various principles, I think there are eight principles or criteria, to ensure successful command and control. I just read them out: "Objectives, authority, responsibility, trust, discipline, morale, regulations, and time." Are these principles equally encapsulated in developed armies within your professional experience?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: In different words, they are very similar, and are stressed in -- in certainly British doctrine and other European armies' doctrine, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how important are they for the establishment of command and control?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, they're plainly important. And if I quote from my own report and pick out one or two -- take authority, for example. Under authority, the JNA doctrine discusses reputation and personal authority and goes on to lay out a number of important character traits required for effective command. These include honesty, truthfulness, expertise, and familiarity with the job. It goes on to say: "A responsible officer must be knowledgeable about military regulations and must adhere to them." It talks about moral responsibility as being the most prominent form of responsibility assumed by senior military officers. It describes discipline in readily recognisable terms as permeating all interpersonal relations and spreading across the entire organisation, and it stresses the importance of self-discipline. So all of this is readily recognisable in European doctrines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Again, moving on to paragraph 19 of your report. If I summarise it, it deals with the command at brigade level, and the discussion is in the JNA 1984 brigade rules. Could I ask the Court, please, to turn to footnote 12 and 13 as I want to deal with two topics there. 11 really is just the frontispiece. May I deal with footnote 12. It should have "Introduction." Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we go to the bottom of the page, it is ostensibly the third paragraph from the end. It commences: "The aim of the rules." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you kind enough, please, to read that and then I will deal with other matters?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: The paragraph reads: "The aim of the rules is to ensure that each separate brigade, according to its purpose and capabilities, adopt and apply unified views, attitudes and tactical moves in the preparation, organisation and execution of combat operations in an All People's Defence war." It goes on: "It is a duty of all senior staff and commands to study the provision of these rules in detail and to test and evaluate them during training for all types of brigades and for the conditions in which they operate."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps an overly simplistic question, but how important is it for officers or commanders to familiarise themselves with the rules in respect of command and control?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: It's very important. And it's not really a question of rules, it's a question of doctrine and training. Officers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down for the benefit of the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officers are taught and brought up to apply the doctrine applicable in order that when orders are given there is a clear understanding of what they mean and the sort of actions that they imply, and the sort of way that those orders would be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And may we deal with footnote 13, please. There should be reference to chapter IV, the heading of "Command and joint provisions." Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I really want to deal or focus on one section, which is paragraph 107. Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to read that out?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Paragraph 107 reads: "Command of the brigade is part of an integrated system of command and control, which is based on adopted principles of command. Command implies the best ways of using human skills and the capabilities of equipment for the brigade to achieve the best possible results in performing a given task. To this end, command must be integrated, continuous, secure, flexible, effective and operational."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you agree with that particular analysis of command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, that is readily recognisable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it recognisable within other armies within your experience?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. In my own army, for example, that is readily understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to move to paragraph 20, if I may, please, of the report. You have already dealt with it, and perhaps if I can abbreviate it in the following way: That you came to the conclusion that this document was a comprehensive, sound and well-written command and control doctrine which lay down the principles and fundamentals with which all officers are required to be familiar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, that was the opinion I came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to move to a new topic, if I may, please, which really relates to the application of command and control principles vis-a-vis Operation Group South. May I refer you, please, to your paragraph 21. In the report itself, there is actually highlighted a question which I will read into the record, and then deal with it in a moment. Question based on the 1st Military District and OG South documents that you were shown by the Prosecution, describe how these principles of command and control were applied by the commander of the JNA OG South during the Vukovar operations. So we deal with the application, as I have already indicated. May I just deal with it in this way: We know that OG South had both regular JNA units as well as reserve and paramilitary/volunteer units. From the documentation that you have seen but more particularly from the experience that you have gained over your period in the military, are you able to conclude if there was proper application of JNA principles regarding command and control in respect of these subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. From the documents I have read, starting with the doctrine and then going on to Operations Group South orders and reports and other documents such as war journals and diaries, it's clear to me that there was a functioning command and control system with information and orders flowing down the chain of command and information flowing up the chain of command, and that's exactly what I would expect. It's what the doctrine lays down, and it's what -- and it's how a well-trained unit like the Guards Motorised Brigade would be expected to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with paragraph 24, but perhaps for completeness sake the conclusion that you have given, I think it's right to say for brevity's sake you have referred to paragraphs 22, or there is reference in paragraph 22 and 23 of some of the documentation that you have perused when evaluating this particular topic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That is correct. And I think I've footnoted them as 15, 16, 17, 18, to 20 on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not going to use time in relation to those documents. They're available to you, and if cross-examination is required, they are available. May we deal then, please, with paragraph 24 of your report. Here there is reference to what is called an assault detachment. Again, for the assistance of all parties, what is an assault detachment, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yeah. Your Honour, I understand an assault detachment to be temporary combat units made up of a variety of troops; infantry, armour, engineers, military police, pioneers, whatever is required to achieve the task. All those troops would be under the command of a single overall commander, that is the assault detachment commander. And an assault detachment could be divided into a number of smaller groups which are termed in JNA doctrine "assault groups." Now, those mixed or what we would describe as all-arms groupings are very akin to what in NATO armies are described as battle groups, which are formations made up of a number of different arms, and by arms, I mean infantry, armour, engineers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the material available to you, are you able to say if the -- the TO and volunteer units were integrated into the assault detachments of OG South?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen a number of orders in which the distribution lists include TO and volunteer units and orders given to assault detachments whose composition includes TO and volunteer units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Again, dealing with the application of the command and control principles, to what extent does a commander have to be aware of the - my words - possible variability of disciplinary levels in units subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, we've touched on this already, and it comes back to a commander's accountability and responsibility for everything that happens in his command and by those whom he commands. Therefore, the implication of that is that a commander must have a good feel for the capabilities of those he commands which, as the groupings become more varied, such as assault detachments and assault groups, becomes even more important. If those groupings include other than well-trained regular troops, less well-trained TO troops and volunteers whose training may not be apparent to the commander at all, then he has an absolute responsibility to ensure that, (a), he has -- he understands what their capabilities are, what their level of discipline is, how they operate in order to be able to, (a), control them, and (b), give them appropriate - and I stress the word "appropriate" - tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that principle apply to commanders at all levels?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Absolutely. That principle would apply at an assault group level, at an assault detachment level, or OG South level for that matter, where the groupings are made up of different sorts of troops with different capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to move on to paragraph 27 of your report. Here you deal specifically with the competence and perhaps requirements for the suitability of the position of commander of OG South. My first question would be this: On your own experience or from your own experience, what level of competence was required to be appointed commander of a guards, or the guards brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I read the Guards Motorised Brigade as the elite formation of the JNA. It was better equipped, better organised, had higher standards, better training, than the more run-of-the-mill units of the JNA. To command that organisation would have required, in my professional opinion, an extremely high-grade officer, specifically selected for the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I deal with a topic that's often called situational awareness. From the documents that you have seen, are you able to indicate the level of situational awareness existing within the command structure of OG South?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. Referring to the orders and reports that I have read and the war journal and operational diaries, it's clear that there was a well-tried and exercised system for passing information up and down the chain of command, using a variety of methods from routine reporting, radio reporting, liaison officers, visits, all of which would be normal, and all of which would end up with the commander having a proper and full situational awareness, both from his own actions and from the process of information being passed to him by his staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why is situational awareness important in a command structure?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, situational awareness is important, per se, because unless the commander is fully aware of what's happening around him, both from the enemy forces and own forces situation, he will not be able to make the correct decisions or take the correct actions required for his responsibilities and accountabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how does a commander achieve situational awareness, within your experience?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, as I've touched on, there's obviously the normal reporting regime, where he is assist -- where reports are coming into his headquarters, both over the radio and through liaison visits and -- and officers reporting in. But also a responsible commander would not just sit in his headquarters and rely on information to be fed to him. He would be actively pursuing the sort of information he wanted. He would be visiting those commanders subordinated to him, looking them in the eye, judging what they're saying, seeing what their sense of morale is, assessing for himself whether there are any problems that may not have come to the attention of the staff that need addressing. All of that will result in the commander having a full, as you describe it, situational awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with a very small topic. It's quite simply this: What is the function of a duty officer?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, a duty officer, as his name implies, is on duty to carry out a specific function. It would normally -- for example, in a brigade headquarters, duty officers would be manning the operations desks or the desks for the other functions of command, receiving information, assessing it, taking actions where he -- on his own initiative where he was empowered to do so, or where appropriate, and, in particular, making sure that the commander and/or the Chief of Staff were fully appraised of anything that he thought they should be appraised of immediately, if it was urgent, or routinely through situational updates, et cetera, if it wasn't urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To what extent -- or perhaps how important is it for a record, a documentary record to be kept in relation to important material, given either to a duty officer or indeed to a command itself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, that's important. You will recall that one of the principles of command was continuity. Now, this implies that whoever is -- amongst other things, whoever is on duty there must be a continuous actioning and responsibility for what is happening. And therefore, the way that that is done, because duty officers cannot be on duty forever, and there would be a shift system, important information is recorded, and when one duty officer hands over to another, they will go over the important aspects and those aspects that need following up in the new duty officer's watch. It's also important so that there is a note or a record of information that needs to be passed to the Chief of Staff or the commander or that they can simply call for the log and skim through it, read through it themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to try and merge, if I may, the topic of commander and record, in relation to an issue of subordination and resubordination. As a commander, to what extent or perhaps again how important is it for a record to be kept of the resubordination of a unit that had been previously subordinated to you as a commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, that's important for a number of reasons. If a unit is resubordinated, that could carry with it command and control implications, it could carry with it logistic implications. It might mean that logistic resources or resupply of, for example, ammunition, food, water, fuel, needs to be switched in another direction. So it's clear, must be clear that certainly all the staff and particularly the supporting commanders, by which I mean the logistic commanders, the artillery commanders, the engineer commanders know who is subordinated at a certain time or resubordinated at a certain time so that they can control and organise the support that they are providing appropriately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If this is not done, what are the possible consequences in relation to command and control?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: If it's not done, the consequences are confusion. You may get the wrong orders or inappropriate orders going down the chain of command on the assumption that it is going to an organisation comprising of a certain organisation, when, in fact, it's not because some of that organisation has been taken out and put somewhere else. So it -- it's important in that respect. But it's also important in terms of logistic resupply. If it's not clear, as I said, to the supporting commanders who is where in the organisation, they cannot plan their logistic support appropriately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move on to a new topic. I would, if Your Honour wouldn't mind, wish to take a break at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the 20-minute break now, Mr. Moore, and then resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that Mr. Lukic may have an application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's not an application, but you know the position that my team is in; we're last when it comes to cross-examination. So what I would like to know is the exact rules of the game as far as the cross-examination of this witness is concerned, or the examination, we would like to know how long the in-chief would last and how long the three teams are going to have. So could you please provide clear guide-lines for us, because, if possible, it would be helpful for us to know all of this now. It's up to the Chamber, of course. And I don't know, perhaps it would be possible also if the witness is available, and if the Trial Chamber is willing, that we perhaps continue to work for part of the afternoon tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer is that you will have two hours, each Defence team. And the Prosecution has a slight more flexibility. It will run over two hours in-chief, but only a little. But you will each have two hours, so a total of six hours between the three of you, okay? And it will all conclude by 1345 tomorrow. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you understand your batting order there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm trying to work out the -- the timetable, but I anticipate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will finish at about midday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But as I've indicated, you can stretch over, because if you stretch over, you're merely diminishing your own re-examination time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we're being very generous to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Without hesitation, if I may move on then, please, to the issue of notice. You deal with it in paragraph 32 of your report. You have already informed us about situations in which you have been involved where, to use your phrase, there was terrorism, namely Northern Ireland, military conflict, perhaps within the Balkans. Now, when one has a situation where you have irregularity within the combat, if there is such a thing, does that create difficulties over and above what I will call normal combat tensions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Define irregularities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Defining irregularities to this extent: If one looks at a war between two disciplined armies, one I would suggest probably expects a level of consistency in relation to tensions that may exist between those two conflicting parties. If one moves to scenario two, here you may have, as was in Northern Ireland, conflict between paramilitaries of Protestant, Catholic; in the Balkans you had irregular forces as well on either side. What I would like to know is if one deals with what I will call localised combat, does that create any additional difficulties over and above that which one would normally expect?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, the situation is plainly more complex, but the laws of armed conflict would apply in exactly the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To what extent should a commander of whatever level be aware of the dangers of unlawful acts to units subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, he's got to be -- he's got to be absolutely aware because he is accountable. And that goes back to my previous answers about knowing the capabilities or shortcomings of those under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What could or should a commander do to avoid such problems or eliminate such possible dangers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, the sort of actions he could take would be to ensure that less well-trained troops, such as TO or irregulars or volunteers, are placed firmly within the chain of command with a responsible commander who is given clear direction to ensure that these less well-trained troops are tasked appropriately and behave appropriately and to report back if there are any problems in that respect. So that's one thing he can do. He can also take a very personal view himself and ensure by visits that that is happening and be aware of -- of the dangers in which he himself will find -- in which he will find himself, as he is accountable for their actions as they are under his command. He can take a very personal interest in these particular sorts of troops, how they're tasked, how they're involved, and how they're performing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to, please, at footnote 39 bis. It is also Exhibit 415. It's a document of the 18th of November. It is a document that has been signed by Lieutenant-General Zivota Panic. It should be under footnote 39 bis. Have you got that document, General?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to deal with it in a moment, if I may, please. Let us look at this document. I'll deal with it initially in a fairly brief way. We have got the date, top left-hand corner, 18th of November, 1991. We have got just below that the phrase, "Very urgent." Below that, "Deliver immediately." And we can see to whom it is sent, and we can see on the second line of the recipients, OG South. Now, I want to deal with various parts of this document, please. If we look at the bottom of the page, it is page 1 in the middle. We can see the penultimate paragraph commencing, "However, the war." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will read that and then I will move on to another part of the document. "However, the war did not end with the fall of Vukovar and an even more fierce and brutal war against Ustasha forces is now ahead of us." Can we then turn over the page, please? And I want to deal with again two parts of this page. First it relates to order. One is OG South. Moving to the very bottom of that page: "While carrying out these assignments," it clearly relates to OG South and North, "and in other operations in the area in which first VO units are engaged on smashing Ustasha forces, observe all aspects of the Geneva Convention on prisoners of war." Now, I'd like to turn over, please, to the final page of that document. And it is number 8. Would you be kind enough, please, to read out that particular paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 of this order reads: "Every unit must fully control the situation on the territory of its area of responsibility. Commanders at all levels will be responsible for this. Wartime laws have not entered into force, and therefore, as always, nobody has the right to retribution and other kinds of revenge which some local TO Territorial Defence units carried out. In future, arrest those who commit any such acts and undertake appropriate legal measures."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to the following questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies for interrupting my learned friend, but this reference cited in his question, I'm afraid I am unable to find it in this order that we are talking about. Perhaps my learned friend can tell me where it states that it is ordered -- just one moment. "[Previous translation continues] ... [In English] ... situation on the territory of its area of responsibility [Interpretation] in relations to Operations Group South, and that the applications of the Geneva Conventions is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I obviously work from the English translation, and I think that -- well, it has already been an exhibit. I have it clearly on page 1 who the recipients are. Order is in relation to page 2, and clearly the recipient is OG South. The reference to "observe all aspects of the Geneva Convention on the prisoners of war" is my page 2, the bottom of the English. There is a reference, actually, to "prevent any disobedience of unsoldierly appearance of behaviour" on page 3. And I've got, as indeed the General has read out, paragraph 8, and I only want to move on to Zivota Panic. Has my learned friend now located that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: General, and clearly we see the signatory is Lieutenant-General Zivota Panic. The questions that I have in relation to this and the topic of notice are as follows: Does such a document properly reflect the concerns of a commander in a way that is appropriate for the circumstances existing after the conclusion of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Absolutely. This is -- this is an order from General Panic to his subordinate commanders, including Colonel Mrksic, commander Operations Group South, which will be like a flashing beacon to the recipients, because it will be quite clear from the tone and the content that their superior commander is extremely concerned that, given the situation, atrocities, shall I put it like that, or acts in contravention of the Geneva Conventions on the prisoners of war could occur, and he is saying to his subordinate commanders, I want you to pay particular personal attention to this issue and ensure that it does not. And he goes on to say that it has already happened with some local TO Territorial Defence units. So a recipient receiving this order would take this extremely seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I just move on to the next question. If you received such an order from your superior commander, what steps and/or measures would you take to carry out the directions of your commander as a result of the receipt of this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I would immediately translate this into an order of my own, reflecting my commander's concerns, adding whatever flavour of my own I wished to. I would draw particular attention to the close supervision required of TO units and volunteers in my command, and I would probably go visiting forward to look commanders in the eye and impress them of the urgency of this order and what I expected them to do to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why would you do such a thing, or why would you implement orders in that way?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I would implement them in the first -- in the first instance because my commander is plainly concerned and has brought it to my attention, and therefore it is my responsibility to act; and secondly, I would do it because I would realise that I am accountable for my actions. And if there are such actions, if such acts occur in my area of responsibility, it will be my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Not the least of which, it is against, and I would realise it, it is against the international laws of war, to which we have subscribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you seen any document, documents or orders that is consistent with the urgency of this order from Zivota Panic passing on these concerns?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: In the documents that I have been provided with, I have not noticed the sort of actions logged as I have described. I have noted, I think it's in the war journal, the receipt of this document. But interestingly, if I remember rightly, in the actions column there's no comment. There's no comment to the effect that commander impressed this on all subordinates, or orders group called to impress on all subordinates Geneva Conventions, or even commander visited forward to impress this order on subordinate. There's not -- I've come across no "action on" comments. All I've seen is that that order was noted as received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to deal with an issue that I will call verbal notice. If a commander of whatever level receives information that illegal acts are occurring or are about to occur, does he have a duty to act?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: He has an absolute duty to act. And it is laid down, inter alia, in the JNA doctrine on compliance with the International Laws of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If that officer fails to act immediately, does that diminish the duty that he has in relation to that notice given?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, he would be well advised to act immediately. Because he would realise that he is accountable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That deals with the subject if acts are occurring or about to occur. Let us move on to a slight variation of that. If a commander, at whatever level, receives information that illegal acts have already occurred, does he have a duty to act?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, he does. As, for example, General Panic has acted in putting out his own order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what should that commander do, in your professional opinion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: He should -- first of all, if it is -- if it is clearly who has carried out these acts, they should be arrested immediately. If it is not clear who has carried out these acts, he should institute an immediate investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I wish to deal now with the topic of evacuation. I hope it is paragraphs 68 to 76. Again, I will read into the record the formal question that you were asked. "Evacuation operations. Drawing from your knowledge of (international) regulations and your military experience, explain, by ways of a generic example, how a commander should plan, organise, and carry out the evacuation of prisoners from a protected facility (for example a hospital) through hostile territory, that was agreed upon at a higher level." Now, I want to deal with that topic, if I may. In your report you state that given the existing circumstances at that time, such an evacuation, in this case of the hospital, would constitute a very high-profile event. I think that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you and do you consider it was a high-profile event?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I consider this evacuation to be a high-profile event for a number of reasons. Starting with the fact that it emanated from something that I understand was called the Zagreb agreement, which was agreed at very high level between the two states concerned. And secondly, it's going to be a high-profile event because that agreement involved the close monitoring of this operation by international agencies such as the Red Cross. And thirdly, given the events that have just occurred, a very hard-fought battle for Vukovar, a lot of loss of life, lots of wounded, a confused situation, the existence in my command of TO and volunteer units who I have already been warned of their activities elsewhere, and the implications on my part to ensure that the Geneva Conventions are strictly adhered to by my superior commander, I would be under absolutely no delusion at all that this was an operation in which I would have to take a very, very personal interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. The following questions in relation to this topic: Firstly, would you expect a commander to be aware of or indeed possibly involved in such an evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, the commander could not possibly be unaware of the evacuation, because it is a major operation occurring in his area of responsibility. So it is inconceivable that he would be unaware of it. Being aware of it, for the reasons I have just said, I would expect the commander to, with his staff, plan and issue the orders for what is, in effect, a very complex operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. By delegating or by delegation of the organisational role for that evacuation, does this diminish the commander's obligation to ensure its successful completion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The commander is fully responsible for everything that happens under his command, by those under his command, in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. If a superior officer/commander delegates the task of the evacuation operation to a subordinate officer, to what extent does such delegation diminish the duties of that subordinated officer in the performance of his tasks?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: The officer to whom the task has been subordinated will be responsible for the proper conduct of the task and accountable to his commander for the proper conduct of the task. The commander will remain responsible as the commander for the way in which that task is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If I use the word "command," simpliciter, what does it mean in the military context, what, in your judgement would be the hallmarks of command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
