utterances.text: As I said in paragraph 16 of my report, command and control, command really involves leadership and decision-making, and therefore involves planning and giving orders with the expectation that subordinates will carry them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Given your professional experience and the complexity of the evacuation operation, would you expect a written order to be issued?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I certainly would. Because this operation is going to involve a whole host of different units under my command. There are going to be logistic implications. There's going to be transport required. There's going to be guarding required. There's going to be security organ activities in terms of sorting out who's who. There's going to be route clearance. It's a highly complex operation. There's not to mention the fact that it's going to be observed by international organisations which will need liaison and monitoring in their own right. And therefore, that, in the normal course of events, would be the subject of an operation order declaring how that operation is going to be carried out, who's in command, and issuing tasks to the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. In the carrying out of such an evacuation operation, to what extent should the commanding officer take appropriate steps to ensure the safety of the evacuees?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, the whole -- that is the responsibility of the whole of the chain of command, and in -- in this instance, from the commander of OG South downwards, the commander of OG South would be impressing on whoever he has delegated responsibility for the evacuation, his responsibilities towards the safety of the evacuees, and the officer and everybody involved in the evacuation would also be responsible for ensuring the safety of the evacuees. But in particular, the commanding officer of the evacuation operation itself would have an absolute responsibility to ensure that all the forces he is commanding, conducting the operation, are briefed properly in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. If a commander of whatever level has information that atrocities either have or may occur, how would that affect the planning of the evacuation operation and, above all, the successful completion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, if a commander, or the commander, is aware that troops under his command have already carried out that sort of act, then he would be alert to that fact and would ensure that those troops were not in any way involved in such a delicate operation. If that had not occurred, but knowing that TO units and volunteer units were in the area, even if not involved in the operation directly, but maybe they were, or could be, then he would be impressing down the chain of command the -- what he expected from his subordinate commanders in that -- in that respect in exactly the same way as General Panic has done to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to deal with a topic that I will label "zone of responsibility." Do you agree with the following hypothesis: That a commander cannot delegate command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: If you mean by that does the responsibility of a higher commander cease to exist when he has delegated tasks to a subordinate commander, the answer to that is no. The responsibility remains with commanders at all levels, and the higher commander remains responsible for all actions carried out to delegate its subordinates within their own areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to try and deal with a topic, for the assistance of all parties, and deal with it as neutrally as I possibly can. We have a situation evidentially in this case that on the 20th of November, 1991 Ovcara was located in the zone of responsibility of the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade; that's Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. The 80th Motorised Brigade is and was subordinated to OG South. There is evidence that a Major Vukasinovic, a security organ within the command of OG South, entered the zone of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Thirdly, we have evidence that incidents apparently were occurring at that time at Ovcara. Now, Vojnovic was asked why he did not deal with the problem immediately in what I will call a military sense, and he stated as follows, and I summarise it, that a member of the superior command had entered his zone of responsibility without notifying him. And he stated that he subsequently went to Mrksic to inform him. Now, what is the responsibility of Mrksic for -- or shall I not personalise it. What is the -- what is the responsibility of the superior commander for events that have occurred within the zone of responsibility of his subordinate unit?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, it would be clear to the superior commander that there was a command and control muddle here. You will recall the principle of unity of command. Here we have an officer responsible for a zone of responsibility, or an area of responsibility, who has found another organisation carrying out an operation in his area without, apparently, his knowledge or without, apparently, him being involved in the planning or the orders for that operation. Moreover, this operation being carried out in his area of -- in his area of responsibility appears to be being carried out by officers from the brigade staff. So, in my view, what he did was absolutely correct. He went to his commander and said, There is an absolute muddle going on here, what is your direction, commander, to sort it out. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It does. Thank you very much. I am almost out of time. On the material that you have had available to you, are you able to indicate to the Court whether Colonel Mrksic or his conduct achieved the level one would expect from an officer in his position?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, from the material that has been made available to me, I conclude that the commander of OG South failed to take the sort of actions that I would have expected from a commander of his standing and experience, and which, in my opinion, that failure has contributed to the events that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To assist the Court, one really refers to paragraph 81 of the report. May I deal with paragraph 82, when you move on to Major Sljivancanin. I want to read out the second sentence. There's reference to personal involvement. And then following this -- following that, I should say: "Furthermore, he, Sljivancanin, appears to have played a greater command role in organising and conducting the evacuation of the hospital than might be expected from an officer of his appointment." Why do you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I came to that conclusion from reading the documents which I was provided with, which indicated to me that Major Sljivancanin was very personally involved in the evacuation of the hospital; in particular, giving orders and directing and being seen around at all times, and for -- to all extent and purposes, giving the appearance that, from what I read, that he was in command and able to direct subordinate units to act in accordance with what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention, please, to the following page, page 29. It is the final -- final sentence of that paragraph, paragraph 83, commencing: "His failure to take effective appropriate action before, during or after the events, which are the subject of the indictment, to ensure proper conduct all indicates to me that Major Sljivancanin failed to act in accordance with JNA doctrine and failed in his duty as an officer and as a senior advisor to Colonel Mile Mrksic, his commander." Why do you come to that conclusion? What is that conclusion based upon?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's based on the documentation that I have read. And to give you an example, it would appear to me that Major Sljivancanin was in charge of the evacuation operation. It would appear to me that he was fully aware of the everything that was happening and that happened. He was fully aware that there were TO and volunteer forces involved. He was fully aware of their conduct. And all of that is -- and the conduct of that operation was as far from compliance with JNA doctrine that I can imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal, please, with Captain Miroslav Radic. It's paragraphs 84 to 86. Again, I will attempt to abbreviate. Paragraph 86: "Captain Miroslav Radic's failure to take it effective appropriate action before, during or after the events, which are the subject of the indictment, to ensure proper conduct in the evacuation operation, or to instigate appropriate disciplinary investigations after becoming aware of the massacre of the prisoners of war by TO and volunteer troops then under his command, in my opinion indicates that Captain Miroslav Radic failed to act in accordance with JNA doctrine and failed in his duty as an officer and a commander." What do you base that summation upon?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Again, I base that on the documents with which I was provided, which would indicate to me that whilst Captain Radic does not appear to have been present at Ovcara he became fully aware of what had happened at Ovcara, I think the next day, when he was involved, I believe, with conversations with various TO and volunteer elements. And I concluded from that that even if he had not been there he was aware or became aware of what had happened, and therefore in accordance with JNA doctrine, he had a duty to act. He had a duty, immediately, to report that up the chain of command and to investigate and, if necessary, arrest those that he had become aware were suspected of carrying out such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Dealing with Captain Radic, if Captain Radic had been made aware of such incidents at the time that they were occurring, does that strengthen or weaken your conclusion in relation to him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: If he had been made aware that such incidents were occurring at the time they were occurring, it puts even more onus on immediate action, (a), to alert the chain of command, and (b), to take action to stop it. And then subsequently to deal with those perpetrating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much. But I would seek to put the report in as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 600, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And is that in the coloured, final form? Or the original, or what, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is in the coloured form, but with the Court's leave and the agreement, as I'm sure will be the case, of my learned friends, what I intend to do will be to tender the report in an upgraded form --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've mentioned that. My interest is that there is the original report and now a coloured modification of it. Are you wanting both or just one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I explain, I hope simply and fairly, and that is the original report was created in August. Clearly there were witnesses we did not seek to call, and we have supplemented it -- or the General has supplemented it with reference to other documents. Perhaps it would be prudent to put in both reports and that way it avoids any doubt or problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would accord with the Chamber's view of the practical situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive the report in both forms.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report in the original form will be Exhibit 601.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to cross-examine the witness anyway, but I would just like to clarify something in relation to this exhibit tendered just now. It's not clear to me if both of them are accepted, both the expert reports, and one is not underlined, then I don't know what the point would be of this other one being underlined. Are we accepting the first one to see what the original report was, and then those parts that were red-lined will then not be taken into consideration. This is how my learned friend, Mr. Moore, explained it, but I just wanted to clarify it so it's clear to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought we had laboured over that to the point of complete clarity, Mr. Vasic. The original report is the original report and it is received as such. Clearly to the extent at least that it is now underlined in the second version, it's acknowledged by the Prosecution that it has not substantiated parts of the report. The underlined, coloured version, is a practical means of everybody, including the Chamber, being aware and not unconsciously falling into the trap of relying on passages that have not been proved. Is that enough? And the original is received on that basis and with that caveat. Your time starts 10 past midday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Pringle, good afternoon. I'm Miroslav Vasic, and I represent Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. I just received a note. We have not received any lists of exhibits to be used by my learned friends in cross-examination. There may be an error, but if such, I wonder if there is such a list we could have a copy of it, please. For all three defendants.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to make up for what time Mr. Moore has taken up. Some of the documents tendered here as exhibits, I'm going to use them. That is not going to be a problem. My opinion is that this expert expressed his opinion in response to questions by the Prosecutor, so in the same way I'm going to conduct my cross-examination, at least as far as I'm concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure that Mr. Lukic and Mr. Borovic, if they're going to rely upon documents, will ensure that Mr. Moore has a list over the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, you said in your report that you approached your task when the Prosecution asked you for assistance in the Vukovar case by providing your assessment of the evolution of the military and professional aspect of this case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you then provided with the complete documentation in the possession of the Prosecution, and were you in the position to pick from those documents those documents that you mentioned in Annex A, attached to your report, or were you presented only with the documents that you note in the annex?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I was presented with the documents noted in the annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I also have a question about the annex. In the annex you list 60 witness names whose statements you received from my learned friends from the Prosecution. What I would like to know is whether you also received transcripts of the testimony of those witnesses who testified in this case and who are on the list, and -- or you only received the transcripts provided to you by my learned friend which he believed to be relevant for your expert testimony?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I received the transcripts of the list of witnesses at the annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did my friend from the Prosecution draw your attention to the differences in the statements of certain witnesses and what they testified before the Trial Chamber, or did you actually go through the transcripts and find the differences yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I went through the transcripts myself in the process of compiling my report, and indeed the statements in my report and the conclusions drawn were as a result of reading the documents annexed in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to ask you that now that you are aware of the differences in the statements, in the transcript, and from the witness statements, did you completely disregard those differences in your findings, or are there still some parts in your findings other than what was underlined by my learned friend that he did not seek to rely upon?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand you where you say that you are aware of the differences in the statements in the transcript, and from the witness statements. The witness -- I read the transcripts of the witness statements in the annex. I'm sorry, Mr. Vasic, I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm going to clarify my question; it wasn't entirely clear. When I say "transcript," that is the transcript of the live testimony of a witness in this courtroom before this Trial Chamber. So in cases you found that the transcript of a certain witness was different in comparison to the statement that he gave to the Prosecution investigators, for example, did you then leave such a statement out of your findings? That's my question. I think I've been a bit clearer now.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I think I can see where you're getting at. My report was written based on the witness statements as they were in the annex when I received them. I believe subsequent to that various witnesses did give testimony. I was provided with some testimony. For example, I was provided with -- I think it's Major Trifunovic, his testimony which I read. I'm not aware which of these witnesses in totality have given evidence and which haven't, but I have -- I have read some testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, I would like to ask you to make the effort now and to recall other than the transcript of Mr. Trifunovic, do you recall the names of any other witnesses whose testimony transcript you've read while drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. I have read -- remind me of the name of the commander of 80 MBTR? Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Vojnovic, I have read that. I've read his testimony. Yeah, in court. I've read, I think, Vucic, number 72. I'm trying to recall the difference between testimony and original witness statement. But I have read some, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pringle. I see that in Annex A there are 60 names whose statements you received. As far as I was able to analyse, in drafting your report you used about 20 per cent of these statements; the rest you did not use. Could you please tell us what criteria you used to decide to use these 20 per cent and not to use the 80 per cent? Was that your own criteria, or was it done in that way for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: No, it was my own criteria, and you will see in my report it's broken up into a number of questions highlighted in bold print. And I was looking for statements and evidence, if that's the right word, that would help me answer those questions. And not all of it was relevant to those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It's as if you guessed, actually, what I am interested in, whether your research of the material was limited by the questions that were put to you. You didn't go beyond the strict confines of these questions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's partly correct and partly incorrect. My research of the material was not limited by the questions. My answering of the questions was drawn from the material that I read, not all of which was relevant to answering the specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand, thank you. According to you, all the relevant materials that you read are included in your report, which you considered to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: All the relevant materials were included in my research. I then drew on that research to answer the questions in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The relevant parts that you found while reviewing the documents before drafting the report are all included in the report. None of them were excluded or left out from the report. This is what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I've drawn on what I have read and footnoted, where appropriate, quoted in some cases, where appropriate. And anything that I have footnoted or quoted has been drawn from the documentation which I was provided with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume that your view or your conclusion which is based -- which is actually evident from your report, is a collection of premises arising from a limited number of documents that you had access to and witness statements shown to you by my learned friends from the Prosecution. So I assume that you would, because of that, agree with me that if you had perhaps had some other documents or other testimonies or statements which would be opposite to the ones you had now, your view or opinion would be subject to change, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Can I refer you to paragraph 3 of my introduction? And I'll read it out for ease. And what I've said is: "I've been asked to consider a number of specific questions which I have addressed below, and if deemed appropriate on the materials supplied to me, to come to a conclusion based on my own experience regarding the military participation and conduct of the three defendants on the subject matter of this indictment." So my report and my conclusions are based on the material I have read. Hypothetically, if I had read something else, I might have come to a different conclusion. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pringle. I would now like to clear up some terminology issues which I think are not quite clear in your findings. In the command and control section you cited, this is paragraph 15, page 4, you say that there was a legal and constitutional basis codified in the SFRY doctrine. My question is: What would the SFRY doctrine be, what would it constitute, since that category actually did not exist in our -- in the time that we are talking about, neither as a concept or a document. This is on page 4 of the English version, paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Vasic, that the 1982 Law on All People's Defence did not exist in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pringle. I'm confused by the term or a concept you use here, and that is the doctrine of the SFRY. I am not familiar with that term or a document. So this is why I would like you to explain what SFRY doctrine means.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Okay. Doctrine. Doctrine at its simplest is what is taught. Doctrine is what is used to describe the base documents on which conduct and procedures, for example, in the military, are carried out. So doctrine in this respect is my terminology. I have described it as JNA doctrine in exactly the same way as I would describe similar documents from other armies as German doctrine, British doctrine, American doctrine, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was a kind of slip or a lapse here? So it's not a doctrine of the JNA, but a doctrine of the SFRY. Now from your answer I assume that what you meant was the doctrine of the Yugoslav People's Army, actually, here, even though it doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, the documents I read were from a large number of sources. I mean, if you take the -- for example, the Law on All People's Defence, that is -- what would you call that, as SFRY doctrine. I would call command and control doctrine that we've talked about into these various pamphlets as JNA doctrine. The word "doctrine" meaning -- being a generic description of what is laid down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pringle, there is no problem in understanding the word "doctrine," but in your findings you link the term "doctrine" with the state, and this term was not familiar. Is this -- what I meant was, actually, the doctrine of the JNA. Do you differentiate between the doctrinal documents, and the normative framework of normative documents when you talk about the system of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I regard the documentation that I have read as completely relevant to the conduct of operations by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in 1991 the JNA doctrine did not exist. What did exist was the doctrine of All People's Defence and social self-protection as a common doctrine of the country's defence system?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: What I would agree is that in 1991 the state of the former Yugoslavia was in the process of dissolution, and therefore the doctrine applied by the JNA would have been drawn on or would have been in compliance with whatever doctrine they had been previously complying with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And my last question before the break is: When you were drafting your expert report, and when you discussed doctrine, did you acquaint yourself with two doctrine documents, the doctrine of All People's Defence and social self-protection, that is the strategy of All People's Defence and social self-protection, and the strategy of armed conflict. Is that something that you incorporated in your expert findings?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I don't believe I have seen either of those documents, unless you can help me, Mr. Vasic. If they're referenced in any one of 100 and something or other footnotes, please draw my attention to them. If they're not there, then I probably haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pringle. They are not there. These are doctrinal documents, and I think that in your findings you dealt more with normative documents. Thank you for your answers. I think that it is time now for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. As I indicated yesterday, it will be necessary for me to spend a longer time than usual during this break. And we will resume at 2.15. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I'm sorry to deal with a matter as I'm going to have to, but there has always been a very clear understanding, rulings from the Bench repeatedly, that we should have notice on documents that are to be served. I mentioned this morning that we had received nothing from the Defence again. As a direct consequence, we get documentation coming through. It's for the Court to decide whether it's been done deliberately. It means we can't speak to the witness about the documents and, I'm sorry, it is not acceptable to just give it to us in, I'm afraid, what can only be said flagrant disregard of what the Court has ordered. It disadvantages the Prosecution, it disadvantages the witness, and as I say, the Court's order was quite specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I take it that what you are saying is that you have just received documents that are of factual relevance and of which neither you nor the witness have any advance notice?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I certainly have no advance notice of them. They may be exhibits; I don't know. They just -- they come in, we don't have a chance to even see them. And what happens is quite simply -- my learned friends can roll their eyes all they want. They know perfectly well that this issue has been going on for weeks. Can we please have the document in advance so at least the witness can see exactly what they may or may not be. This is not being done. And I'm not in the position to say exactly what the issues relate to. As far as we are aware, they may well be exhibits. I think there may be a new document. But, as I say, we are supposed to get notice whether in actual fact they're exhibits or not. And it has not been done again. So may I just make my protest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- and that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will see if there is any affect of that by the time of your re-examination tomorrow. Even if you have to lose some sleep. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, let us continue. In your expertise when you spoke about command and control, you talked about the basic principles of command and control, but I think that you did not encompass the system as a whole, its organisation and system of functioning. What I would like to ask you is if you know whether the system of command and control continues at three levels, the strategic, operational, and tactical levels?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Command and control would encompass all those levels, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that if I say that your assessment of the work of the OG South command's work would be valid only if all the war documents of the command were available to you, including the operations diary, the brigade's book of reporting, which records all the events during regular briefings, and only then you would know which orders arrived from the superior commands and which were then transferred into OG South commands to their subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that. I stated at the beginning that my report was based on the documents I have seen and I have read, and my assessment is based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pringle, but we here had the occasion to hear the operations officer, Mr. Trifunovic, who told us that there was an operations and a reporting diary in the brigade, and that orders that arrived were also recorded in them as well as orders that were passed on further, as well as the reports received by OG South from its subordinate units. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your expertise you dealt also with the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital, and you also dealt with the Zagreb agreement, which you described, I assume at the highest level. The materials that you received from my learned friends from the Prosecution for you to analyse, did you find a single assertion or a single document that the OG South command knew about the contents of this agreement or that it had an order from the 1st Military District, its superior command, to act in accordance with this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: You will find in the -- one of these files the Zagreb agreement. That was an agreement pertaining to the evacuation of prisoners of war in the OG South zone of operations. It is inconceivable to me that the commander of OG South and his headquarters would not have been alerted to that agreement and to the requirement to evacuate the personnel in accordance with the Zagreb agreement, as indeed the evacuation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, that is your conclusion, your opinion. All I asked was if you had seen a single document or a single reference that would refer to the command of the 1st Military District sending such an order to the command of OG South regarding the Zagreb agreement. Would you agree with me there are no such references in the material that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I believe that is correct. I don't think I have seen a 1st Military District order to OG South in the material I have. That does not mean that that does or doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Would you agree with me if I were to say that in the formation of operations groups whose formation is regulated by the rules of the corps it is established that an operations group can be formed at the level or by the command of the 1st Military District and that is actually a formation comprising one corps, strengthened by several brigades, or a formation comprising two or three corpses from the same military district, or that it's a formation which can be formed from a number of corps by the General Staff and then that would be an operations group of the General Staff. Would you agree with me that that would be the definition? Other than it being an ad hoc formation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: As far as my understanding goes, an operations group is a formation that is brought together to carry out a specific task in a specific area of responsibility for a specific time, made up of a number of organisations from the level of brigade up. But I wouldn't be too specific on that, because I think operations groups would take the form of several different forms of organisation, depending on the task required.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you talked about the findings and the opinions of your colleague, Mr. Zorc, and I think that this is how he defined the operations group organisation, in the way that I have just presented to you. Do you remember that? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And he talks about the corps level, but -- and when I read that, I sort of put a question mark against that, because that doctrine is really pertaining to, if you like, nation-on-nation war-fighting, I think, and that is not the situation that was going on. Here we had a state of conflict at a lower level, and therefore it was quite conceivable to me that operations groups would be formed as ad hoc groupings made up of a number of different formations at a lower level.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that a brigade is a formation at the tactical level? Is that correct? At the tactical level of the command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Here again, I think the terms tactical, operational and strategic are potentially misleading in these sorts of operations. The operational level is designed to coordinate and carry out tactical actions in a way that achieves the strategic objective. Put simplistically, a brigade would be carrying out tactical operations. But many of the operations that a brigade will be carrying out in this form of conflict have operational and strategic significance and implications. And therefore, a strict definition of operational or tactical, operational and strategic, I personally find unhelpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, I just have to say in regard to your conclusion, and it is your conclusion that this division arises from the system of the way the command and control system functions, and it is inconceivable that a brigade command can successfully command a unit comprising a number of brigades because it simply does not have any functional capacities in order to be able to successfully command at the operational level. It does not have the sufficient number of officers, it doesn't have the sufficient capacities. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Not necessarily. The Guards Motorised Brigade was an elite formation with a strong organisation, a strong commander, well-trained officers, and a well-functioning headquarters. That organisation would, in my opinion, have been well able to take on other formations under command in exactly the same way as, for example, in NATO doctrine, a battle group could be -- could be -- could consist of much more than one battalion, but it would be the battalion commander or the armoured regiment commander that will be -- that would be in command of the grouping. So, no, I do not agree with your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with my assertion that when forming ad hoc units such as operations and tactical groups, there is a rule that if a command of one unit becomes the command of such an ad hoc formation, it has to be strengthened in order to have the required quality to be able to command at the operational level?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That may be so, but that would be the decision of the superior commander; in this case 1st Military District, General Panic. He, I take it, did not consider that that was necessary. He obviously took the view that the Guards Motorised Brigade was well capable of turning itself into an operational group command at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You are probably aware that before the command of the guards brigade turned into the command of OG South, the then existing OG South had a completely independent command headed by Commander Bajo Bojat?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I'm aware that the Guards Motorised Brigade took over the duties of Operational Group South from a previous commander called Bajo Bojat because I think in the war diary there is a reference to Bojat taking his leave and staying farewell and wishing them good luck. What sort of headquarters he had, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Very well. I am asking you all of this in view of the assignments that OG South had after the combat operations ended in Vukovar, and I assume that you know that during those two or three days more -- or several thousand civilians wounded and the sick were evacuated from Vukovar in several batches, and I assume that you know that the Croatian side did not wish to receive these convoys of the Croatian people who were going there, which, at least in my opinion, created considerable difficulties for the command of OG South in the implementation of their other assignments. Are you -- would you share my opinion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I am aware of the generalities of events after -- was it the 18th? When Vukovar was declared to have fallen. And I am aware that there were a number of evacuations taking place, and I am generally aware of the sort of situation that OG South would have found itself in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you think that turning back the convoy to the area of responsibility of OG South, taking care of them and then sending them to new destinations considered -- was considered to be quite a burden for OG South when it was making its daily plan of assignments and keeping in mind all the assignments that it was supposed to carry out.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: No, I think that is well within the capability and capacity of OG South. You must remember that there is a subtle difference between the sort of operations that were being conducted now in Vukovar which were predominantly static. Had OG South been conducting serious manoeuvre operations over large -- over large areas and covering many, many kilometres, the commander of OG South would have had a very, very different problem. As it was, in this operation, the commander of OG South was static, the headquarters was static. There were not -- these were not manoeuvre operations that he was conducting. These might have been complex operations, and there may have been many different sorts of operations. But that was well within the capacity, in my opinion, of Colonel Mrksic and the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are most probably aware that all that had to do with the convoys that we talked about here, the procedure as far as the civilian population was concerned, and the procedure as far as the prisoners of war from Mitnica were concerned, proceeded in the best possible way and that they arrived at their destination not through Croatia because the Croats did not want to receive them, but through Bosnia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Is that a question, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a -- it's a question whether you are aware that the units engaged on these assignments completely implemented the assignment the way they were supposed to and that assistance was provided to all of those people in the necessary manner.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware that other evacuation operations had been carried out in the zone of responsibility of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked about the commander of OG South and his duty to take appropriate steps in relation to all the aspects of the Geneva Conventions, to prevent any occurrences of indiscipline and to inform the -- failure to act in accordance within the guide-lines from General Zivota Panic. I would first like to look at the order, if we can. This is Exhibit 415. My colleague, Mr. Moore, dealt with that today, and you also read parts of it today. If you can now look at the last page of that order. Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Vasic, are you going to put the English version up on my screen, or are you wanting me to find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Perhaps we can look at the English version, since the witness cannot read B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Are you going to put it on the -- ah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we look at page 3? That would be paragraph 8. In the English version I assume that that is on page 2. Yes, that would be paragraph 8. Thank you. Mr. Pringle, in paragraph 8 -- have you found it, do you see it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The first sentence in paragraph 8 concerning the warnings or the caution to prevent retribution, that part -- does not the first sentence of that paragraph state: "Every unit must fully control the situation on the territory of its area of responsibility for which the commanders at all levels will be responsible." And then after that the text that you read out for my learned friend Mr. Moore follows. Do you agree with -- that what I have just read out is what is stated in the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe you will find that I read out the whole of paragraph 8. "Every unit must fully control the situation on the territory of its area of responsibility. Commanders at all levels will be responsible for their ..." And then it goes on. That's what it says, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the implementation of the assignment means that each of the commanders in their area of responsibility were made responsible for that, according to the instruction from the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Here we fall directly into the chain of command. Each commander at each level is responsible for carrying out his duties as described, and each superior commander is equally responsible for the sum of the responsibilities carried out by his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm interested in now is the following: You spoke about this order, and you talked about your conclusion about the conduct of the commander of OG South. You told us that you read Mr. Trifunovic's transcript of his testimony here before this Trial Chamber. If I were to tell you that in his transcript on page 8237, and this is a reference for my learned friends and for the Tribunal, line 1 to 12, if he said that Colonel Mrksic, as commander of OG South, based on orders received from his superior command, drafted these orders into appropriate orders to his subordinate units, would you then allow for the possibility that an order of this kind was conveyed to the units comprising OG South? Are you familiar with this particular piece of testimony by Mr. Trifunovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Trifunovic testified over something like four days, and there were a lot of pages of testimony. But if that's what -- if that's what he said, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: It doesn't -- I should qualify that by saying -- I mean, he's saying that based on orders received from his superior command. He would have received a lot of different orders from his superior command. He drafted these orders into appropriate orders to his subordinate units. Is that a particular statement or is that a general statement, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The reference was that he meant all important orders arriving from the 1st Military District command, the -- and I did give the page and line reference. Now that we're talking about the material that you looked at, and we mentioned this statement, could you please tell me, the Annex A of your findings, I didn't see that any documents from the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade was given to you for your consideration. All I see are orders from the 1st Military District and the command of OG South. Did you perhaps receive such orders and you didn't include them or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: At the time I drafted this report I don't believe I'd seen -- well, I'd seen -- well, witness -- I had witness statement from Witness 70 -- I think we're talking about Milorad Vojnovic, aren't we? So I'd seen a witness statement. Subsequent to that, after I believe he testified here some days ago, I received his testimony, and I did read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about orders of the command of the 80th Brigade, did you receive a single order? I was asking about the orders issued by the commander of the 80th Brigade in the critical time period. Those are the documents that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I don't believe so, unless they're referenced in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, the commander of Operations Group South, with his strictly confidential order 349-1 dated the 9th of November, 1991, and this is Exhibit 374, formed location or local commands in accordance with orders of the corps command. Are you aware of this, Mr. Pringle?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I've seen that order, and it's an order to assault detachments 1 to 5, if my memory serves me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It's an order that, amongst other things, relates to the assault detachments or the local commands in areas of Vukovar, but also refers to the local command in Negoslavci as well as those in the Ovcara, Jakubovac and Grabovo sectors.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that sometime later, after the 17th of November, 1991, the order was augmented in the way that instead of Slobodan Misovic, the commander of Ovcara, Jakubovac and Grabovo, Miodrag Vojnovic was actually appointed instead of Slobodan Misovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I can't say whether I've seen that particular order or not. But if you'd like to put it on the screen I could comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, this does not arise from the order, but the order is mentioned in a command -- in a combat report of OG South sent to the command of the 1st Military District. All I was asking was whether you knew this. But I think that this is not in dispute that the commander Miodrag Vojnovic was also the commander of the Ovcara sector. Actually, I'm interested in something else that we talked about. Are you aware that the order appointing the local commanders also says that the local commanders, in implementing their tasks, should stick to the rules of the garrison and barracks service from the rules of service of the armed forces, that they need to comply with these rules?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: If you'd like to show me that document, I could comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Can we please have Exhibit 374, the English, please. We'll have it on other monitors in a minute, I hope. Oh, there it is. Thank you. Mr. Pringle -- can we just zoom in a little so that Mr. Pringle can read. This is the order appointing the local commands on the 9th of November, 1991. You can see that now, sir, can't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I've got -- I hereby order, paragraph 1, and the top of paragraph 2 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, because we shall have to go to page 2, item 5, which is the relevant portion that I was asking you about, believing that you were familiar with it. Item 5, please, page 2. Mr. Pringle, can you see item 5?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does it not say: "Organise authorities in these areas in line with the OS service regulations and the relevant regulations on service in garrisons and barracks and undertake all measures in order to prevent attacks by sabotage and terrorist groups and the execution of terrorist actions."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In continuation, thank you. "Compiling instructions for work and securing normal conditions for the life and work of the population."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And finally: "Prevent any ill-treatment to the population and local inhabitants and unauthorised entry and searches or apartments and houses."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: It does say that about the population and local inhabitants, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pringle. What I want it know is -- I will. Do you know that pursuant to the rules governing service in the barracks and garrisons a local commander has the duty to ensure discipline, order and proper service in the area covered by his local command. He's also duty-bound to inform all officers passing through his area of responsibility about all these provisions. This is a provision from the rules of service of the armed forces. Is this a provision that you are familiar with, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: In general terms, I'm familiar with that. And what you say as an instruction in rules appears quite reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The local commander lays down the rules in terms of order and discipline in any provisional detention units in his territory, in the area covered by his command. Is this also something you are familiar with, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, if there were detention units, the local commander would be responsible for it, as would his superior commander, and his superior commander up to the top of the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. The order we just read out sees the local commander prohibiting in the strictest possible terms any mistreatment of the local population. Are you familiar with another order along the same lines passed on the 20th of November by the local command? The strictly confidential number is 439-1, and the exhibit number is 419. In this order they refer to strictly confidential 349-1, underlining again the need to prevent any mistreatment of the local population. Are you familiar with this, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Could you put it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Can we please have Exhibit 419, the English, please. There is one thing that I need to say about the transcript, page 67, line 20. The order, the number of the order -- it's fine. It's fine. My apologies. Mr. Pringle, have we got that now?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that order, and I've referred to it in my report at footnote 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever seen the operations log of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I've seen various operations logs. I think the operations log I've seen is OG South. I'm not sure about 80th Motorised Brigade, unless I've referenced it in here. But again if you'd like me to comment on it, please put it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, you would greatly surprise us if you claimed to have seen the OG South operations log. The Defence certainly have not seen it. Nor has Mr. Theunens, apparently. However, could we please have Exhibit 375. I would like to show you a particular entry made to the log of the operation -- of the guards brigade on the 19th of November at 1800 hours. My learned friends are familiar with this particular entry. My apologies, this is the war log. Mr. Pringle -- we need the entry marked as 19th of November, 1800 hours. This is page 10, it should be page 10 in the English. Sir, you see what it says: "During the morning the imprisoned Ustasha were taken to the Sremska Mitrovica prison. There is fighting in the hospital area where the remains of the ZNG and MUP, about 200 of them, are expected to surrender. There was an order to be at the ready in order to organise the guarding of prisoners." My question, sir: Were you familiar with this particular war log entry of the 80th Brigade at the time when you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I've just referred to the annex to my report, and the war diary I record in the annex is the Guards Motorised Brigade. So I'm not aware of this at the time I wrote my report. But could you just go back to paragraph 11 -- or what you have just read out, because I'm not sure it's exactly the same as what you've -- what appears on the transcript. Yes, that. Thank you. "And so it was arranged to be prepared about the organising security of the prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pringle. Let me spare you the effort. We have discussed this before the Trial Chamber. During another witness's appearance, we were looking at the B/C/S, and we were able to ascertain that the actual word used there was, "It was ordered" or, "There was an order" instead of the word "arranged." I think that might be what is confusing you. If the word was, "There was an order," if that was the expression used, would that not mean that the commander of the 80th Brigade was ordered to be at the ready in order to organise the guarding of over 200 prisoners from the ZNG and the MUP from the hospital? Would that not appear to be the inference?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Whether the word is "arranged" or "ordered" this appears to be what I would describe as a warning order to 80th Motorised Brigade to be prepared for the organising security of the prisoners. In other words, the inference there is start using your initiative to get ready for the task, orders to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, would this order be sufficient to influence any further actions taken by the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have already commented on the complexity of that operation, the widely differing sorts of formation and units that will become involved, and therefore as -- therefore, I consider the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade would be awaiting detailed orders from the commander of OG South as to who was to be involved, who was to be in charge, how was it to be conducted, et cetera. This is not an order. This is a warning order; this is be ready for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Pringle, but I'm not sure if you have understood me correctly. I meant as a directive, is this a sufficient directive for him to go on, in a manner of speaking, for him to be ready for a -- an assignment coming his way. Would this not determine his behaviour or his actions in any future assignment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: This would alert him to the possibility that he is going to be required to take part in some shape or form in an evacuation-of-prisoners type operation. It is far short of the detail he requires to be able to properly plan that, but it is sufficient for him to get his thinking cap on and start anticipating in a sensible way using his own experience and initiative and thinking about what might be involved, but this is not sufficient to carry out the task. Doesn't even begin to approach that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What if I told you, Mr. Pringle, that Vojnovic, as the commander of the 80th Brigade, had already carried out this particular task on the 18th and the 19th at Ovcara, where his unit was guarding the captured ZNG and MUP units from Mitnica? Is this something you are aware of? Would that not shed new light on this directive that was sent to him on -- at 1800 hours on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I am generally aware of that, and I'm generally aware that that operation was conducted in good order. So he would be generally aware of the sort of operation that he was being invited to think about, but he wouldn't have any of the details; who, where, how, where to, are international organisations involved, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume you are aware of the fact that on the 20th of November another entry was made at 1800 hours to the operations log of the motorised brigade. This is Exhibit 371. The commander requested that guard shifts be set up in order to secure the captured ZNG and MUP members. For this purpose, people from the brigade and from the military police company were assigned from the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand the question, if indeed it is a question. And also, from what I remember, the context of the evidence was that that entry was a consequence of what Vojnovic found at Ovcara, not of what he had been informed of.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this comment made by my learned friend is utterly disrespectful. It is also leading the witness on what he is expected to say. I don't think that is fair. My question was crystal clear. I was asking the witness whether he was aware of this particular entry. That was all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Vasic, I'm not going to get into the game of keeping ring between you two. But the way you put the question did not fairly represent the evidence, and that clearly has led Mr. Moore to making the comment that he did. What you intended to put may be exactly as you have said, but what actually was said is not a fair representation, and Mr. Moore has corrected it. So we'll carry on now. I gather that the General has been trying to answer you for a few moments. So perhaps he should proceed. But understand, unless you are correct, you can't expect Mr. Moore to sit quiet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could you put Exhibit 371 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Of course, I was just about to. This is the entry, the date is the 20th of November, and the time is 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Could I have it blown up a bit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid we don't have the right entry here. 1600 hours. There, Mr. Pringle, can you see that now?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I see an entry, 1600 hours: "The brigade commander requests that shifts of officers be assigned for guarding the captured ZNG and MUP members and brigade command officers were engaged for this."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on this entry in the war log of the 80th Brigade, do you believe that their assignment was to guard the captured ZNG and MUP members on the 20th of November at 1600 hours at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, it says nothing about Ovcara. I think it is an entry for, you said, the 20th of November at 1600 hours. My instant reaction to that would be that this is a bit late for an operation that started that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, I'm asking you a simple question. If you look at the entry, what do you think? Do you not believe that their assignment was to guard the ZNG prisoners? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. It says: "Assigned for guarding the captured ZNG and MUP members." It doesn't say where.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pringle. But can you please look at the next entry, 2235. What about that entry? Does it not seem to indicate that the location is Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: This says: "The security for the camp for captured ZNG members was withdrawn from the Ovcara sector and this duty was taken over by Vukovar territorials. The" -- not quite sure whether -- is that military police? "... and duty organs from the brigade command returned to the KM in Negoslavci village." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we now agree that this should lead one to conclude that the place where all of this is happening is Ovcara, of all places?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, the entry for 2235 hours does mention the word "Ovcara," I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pringle. Speaking of this entry, the 2235 entry, in your opinion, sir, the officer in charge of securing these prisoners, did this officer act in keeping with the rules of service, if sometime at night he withdrew his unit regardless of the fact whether he had previously received an order or not? But bearing in mind the fact that he knew of aggressive behaviour by certain TO members against the prisoners being held at Ovcara? Would this have been in keeping with the rules of service, the actions taken by this officer? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I have to answer that question in the context of my wider reading. And if I remember rightly, the commander of 80 Motorised Brigade, when he found that brigade staff officers and convoys of buses and prisoners were arriving at Ovcara without his knowledge or previous involvement, went to the Operations Group South command post for the evening orders group at which, if I remember rightly, he arrived late because he had been trying to prevent -- I'm recalling his testimony. He had been trying to prevent what was happening at Ovcara and appeared at OG South where he says to the commander -- or he informs the commander of what is going on at Ovcara. And according to his testimony, he is waved away and dismissed by the commander, which he took to be -- in fact, I think he was asked what are you doing there, according to his testimony - and I'm trying to recall all this - and he took it that the commander's answer and attitude was such that he had no place to be there. And I have to say, in reading that testimony, if you accept that testimony as given, any reasonable commander being alerted to that sort of muddle in command and control that was going on at Ovcara would have taken positive action one way or the other to clear it up, and that doesn't seem to have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, are you saying this based on Mr. Vojnovic's statement, based on his statement that -- based on his inference that he was not supposed to be there, not that he had received any orders or anything, based on his inference that he was entitled to withdraw his unit, having previously witnessed aggressive behaviour displayed by the local TO members against the prisoners there? Is that what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I'm saying that I'm recalling, as best I can, Mr. Vojnovic's testimony in which he drew his superior commander's attention to what was going on at Ovcara and the fact that he found himself in the middle of a command and control muddle. And he -- he testifies to the fact that he got the clear impression that the commander dismissed his concerns; indeed queried what was doing there. What was actually happening was that although Ovcara, I think, was in 80 Motorised Brigade's zone of responsibility, the principle of unity of command had been transgressed in that there was a completely separate operation going on in his area of operations in which he had not been involved and in which he had taken no part in the planning. So he was absolutely right to seek guidance from his commander and having received, in his view -- having received, in his view, from the commander either a dismissal or a why are you involved, took that to mean that he should not be there. And I assume - and it is only an assumption - that that resulted in him withdrawing his troops from Ovcara farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, you have recounted for us the evidence of Mr. Vojnovic. You are a high-ranking officer of the British army. Based on your familiarity with the rules of service, an officer, a brigade commander, the local commander of Jakubovac, Ovcara and Grabovo whose zone of responsibility this happens to be, based just on his own assumption, is he entitled to withdraw his own troops from their assignment of guarding prisoners in the face of the fact that he had previously witnessed an attack by the local TO on these prisoners inside the hangar that night? There had been no orders to this effect, he had received nothing at all. Even if he had received an order along these lines, would he not have had to refuse this order to withdraw his troops? Would that have been in keeping with the rules of service? Would not the same thing apply in the British army, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: My impression is that very little that is happening here is in accordance with the rules of service. What is happening at Ovcara farm is certainly not in accordance with the rules of service. The fact in a commander 80 Motorised Brigade went to his commander to seek guidance and clarification and plainly did not receive it in the way he should have done is a very surprising omission from a commander of Colonel Mrksic's standing and reputation about which one can only surmise, and what you end up with is a complete command and control muddle. So whilst you say, you know, in principle, is this in accordance with regulations, that and everything else that is happening is not in accordance with regulations. The commander of 80 Motorised Brigade, just to finish off, I think must have found himself in a very, very difficult position. And it was his superior commander's responsibility to sort that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, my question was very simple. It was about the rules of service. I reminded you that Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic was the local commander at Ovcara, and we know about his duties as local commander. Would it not be in accordance with the rules of service, would an officer not be duty-bound, an officer unhappy with an order received from his superior, even if there had been an order, an order that might lead to a criminal offence, or even a war crime? Would that officer not have to refuse to carry out this order and go back to his superior officer, ultimately in this case the commander of the 1st Military District? Would that not have been mandated by the rules, or do you see the entire situation in a different light?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: No, the situation I see is one of complete confusion. It's very easy to quote rules. It's extremely difficult in situations like this where an officer finds himself in a state of command and control confusion apparently deliberately unsupported by his superior commander, for him to take the necessary actions. In theory, I suppose Colonel Vojnovic could have mustered the whole of his brigade, gone to Ovcara farm, marched out the TO and volunteers at the point of a gun, and declared operation over. In theory. But it obviously wasn't that easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, I'm not sure if this is something you've heard from my learned friends. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic was the local commander at Ovcara, and between the 15th and the 20th the commander of OG South had resubordinated to him a tactical group of the 125 Brigade, a detachment of the Stara Pazova TO, an armoured battalion belonging to the 544 Motorised Brigade, and this tactical group -- and all of this to set up a security regime in Jakubovac, Ovcara and Grabovo. This unit comprised more than a thousand men. How can you then say that he did not have the right conditions in place to carry out this order issued to him by his own command on the 19th of November at 1800 hours, to go there to take those POWs and to simply guard them? As far as I can see, there is no confusion at all here within the command and control system.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, then, your understanding, Mr. Vasic of command and control is completely different than mine. What a commander 80 Motorised Brigade finds himself in the middle of is the fact that he's been overtaken by events. Had he been given a clear order to conduct the evacuation operation and guard all the prisoners at Ovcara and be responsible for the forces used, he might have been able to decide on his own initiative that the presence of, for example, TO and volunteers was absolutely not in keeping with that sort of operation. But that's not what happened. He was presented with an operation in the course of execution which he then brought to the attention of his commander, and his commander apparently did nothing to sort that out. Now, you can say simplistically, yes, he could then muster his 1.000 men and attack his own side, but if his commander had done nothing to sort it out, that leaves him in a somewhat difficult position. You are trying to shift the responsibility to the commander of 80 Motorised Brigade who has taken the correct action so far and off the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade and OG South who has taken none of the necessary actions required, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I have two questions for you, Mr. Pringle. What you're telling us now, what do you base that on? Where is your opinion founded, in what? Is this all you have to say?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: My opinion, as I have stated, is based on the documentation I have read. Now, I am fully aware that there has been -- that this Court has been sitting for many, many months and I have not seen all the documentation, but based on the documentation I have read, that is my opinion. And it will be for the Court to decide whether my opinion has any veracity or not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Pringle. I will ask you one thing though. Which are the relevant documents that you went through that led you to this inference, with the exception of Mr. Vojnovic's evidence, of course?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I think the key documents are Mr. Vojnovic's evidence, and I think is it -- is it Vasiljevic; is that his name? His testimony -- it's not in my annex because it came in later, but I think his testimony is relevant as well. And the documents I've referenced in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you didn't have a single document from the 80th Brigade, as far as I can tell, based on your report. One thing I'd like to ask you, since you've studied Mr. Vojnovic's statement, since you've based your opinion on that, are you familiar with the fact that Vojnovic claims that after this event at Ovcara on the 21st, once he had found out about these events, he informed no one from his superior command. All he did was held a meeting with his subordinate officer to keep this sort of thing from happening again. That is all he did?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, he had already informed his superior command on, I believe, the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: About what, Mr. Pringle?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: About the events going on at Ovcara farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Which events, Mr. Pringle?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: The events that he describes in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind, your report is based on that testimony. Can you please describe those events for us?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: No, my report was written before I saw his testimony. I only saw his testimony last week or over the last two weeks. Okay, I will recall, I will dredge my memory again. As I recall it, he -- he recalls buses of prisoners arriving at Ovcara farm, he recalls them being made to run the gauntlet, he recalls them being abused, he recalls, if I remember rightly, Major Sljivancanin's presence, he records the presence of TO and volunteers. He describes the placing of a rope in the farm buildings to keep the TO and volunteers who were being extremely threatening to the prisoners apart from the prisoners. He records the presence of brigade staff. Do you want me to go on? He's describing the events at Ovcara farm, which were all most irregular, and which he then, according to his testimony, brought to the attention of his commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As you have just told us, he informed his commander about what he considered to be relevant. I asked you about that bit of information which indicated that people had been killed at Ovcara on the 21st. He did not inform anyone else, those are his own words, with the exception of his directly subordinate officer. Are you familiar with that particular portion of his evidence?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I can't -- I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just another question before -- I'm not sure if it's time for our break. Sir, do you believe that Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, as a -- as the local commander of Ovcara, would have been duty-bound to inform any officer or any institution in his territory about the rules that he had laid down in relation to his own area? Would he not have been duty-bound in keeping with the order from OG South to make sure that those -- that there was no mistreatment of the local population in the area under his command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I agree that commander 80 Motorised Brigade, in carrying out his duties as the -- the local commander would be impressing those -- or should be impressing those sorts of responsibilities under -- to those under his command. What surprises me is that this operation at Ovcara farm was conducted in his area of operations without his knowledge until he came across it and all the events that happened thereafter. So we're addressing two slightly different things here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, to interrupt for one moment. It's the previous question. Is my learned friend, in relation to the composition of the question, at 89:22, is he referring to the order that came in from Zivota Panic where there is a clear indication that the matter should be passed on to subordinate units? Because as far as I'm aware, there is no evidence, as such, apart from speculation, that subsequent -- or subordinate officers were ever informed of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is testimony to show that, as far as I know. I'll try to find the right references. However, this was certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... wish to break now and allow you time to do that? And we will have a 20-minute break and you then have 20 further minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First thing I would like to deal with it what I think I still owe Mr. Moore. The reference in the transcript is 0 -- 9044, lines 16 through 23. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
