utterances.text: Mr. Pringle -- Can we please have Exhibit 425 put on our screens. This is a regular combat report, OG South command, the 22nd of November, 1991. Mr. Pringle, I'm not sure if you're familiar with this, but maybe we're all better off having it on our screens. There is an English translation. Thank you very much. Mr. Pringle, this is a regular combat report dated the 22nd of November. Can we please scroll down to the very end of this report? We'll need to turn the page, please. The last two paragraphs, if we can please blow that up. Mr. Pringle, does it not read: "During the day all measures have been taken related to the 80th Motorised Brigade taking over the organisational and commanding functions in the area of responsibility of Operations Group South." The next passage: "Command of the 80th Motorised Brigade received instructions and documents regarding the organisation of command and control in the area of responsibility of Operations Group South."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic, that's what it says. On an order dated the 22nd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pringle. Based on your experience as a high-ranking military officer, will you agree with me if I say that the conveying of documents and instructions for the organising command and control is the last act in a hand-over between two units?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: This is a -- sorry. I think this is not an order, it's a report, isn't it. It is a report stating that all measures have been undertaken effectively to prepare for 80 Motorised Brigade's takeover, and the final paragraph where it says: "Command of 80 Motorised Brigade received the instructions and documents regarding the organisation of command and control in the area of responsibility of Operations Group South" would indicate to me that we are in the final throes of a hand-over from the guards -- well, from the current Operations Group South, i.e., Guards Motorised Brigade, to 80 Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Pringle. When you were preparing your report, did my learned friend show you any combat reports from the 1st Military District such as those sent to the operations centre of the General Staff on the 20th and 21st of November, 1991. This was in reference to what was going on in the area, including the evacuation? Have you ever seen any of these? The numbers are, if that helps, 1614-177, the date is the 20th of November, and the other is 1614-178. The 21st of December is the date the document bears.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I'm quickly scanning the annex of my report where the documents I received are tabulated. I'm not sure whether they're there or not, to be honest with you. But you'll know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I was just asking whether you were shown these. But my principal question is: Did you ever see anything to indicate that the command of the 1st Military District set up a special team comprising command officers to monitor the evacuation of Vukovar Hospital, the separation of the ZNG and MUP members who were hiding, passing themselves off as patients in the hospital, and sending them to previously determined locations, as well as the general situation. They were supposed to inform the command of the 1st Military District about all these, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That sounds familiar. In the mass of reading I did, I seem to recall something along those lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember whether this team, in their role as monitors, ever established that on the 20th and the 21st the prisoners who were subjected to vetting and triage were sent to certain places and that, in fact, the Geneva Conventions were being complied with, at least as far as they concerned the treatment of POWs? Is this something that you're familiar with, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: No, that's not what I recall. I recall reading quite a lot of witness statements and et cetera to the effect that the prisoners of war being cleared from the hospital were absolutely not being treated in the way that would have been required by the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you base that on the witness statements you read, I suppose. But you don't remember a report like this from the 1st Military District team, just to be clear about this? That's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I do recall, and again this is from memory, a report going upwards to 1st Military District from OG South, I think dated the 20th of November, to the effect that the prisoners of war had been evacuated in strict compliance with the Geneva Conventions, which, as we all know, is not what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, I asked you one thing; you answered a different thing. I'm asking you about this team set up by the command of the 1st Military District to monitor the situation during the evacuation. Do you know whether they stated unequivocally that the Geneva Conventions had been complied with? If yes, please say so. If no, that's no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I don't recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While you were preparing your report, did you ever come across a conclusion by the command of the 1st Military District dated the 21st of November mentioning the fact that certain groups took steps of their own accord, steps that were not in keeping with decisions made by their local commands, and that it was therefore decided that the commands should take appropriate measures to protect the local population from random acts committed by certain groups within their zone of responsibility? Did you ever perhaps come across a reference like this in that conclusion dated the 21st of November in relation to what happened at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I don't recall that, but if you would like to put it on the screen I could comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pringle. I was just asking whether you ever came across anything like that, a document like that. Thank you. Do you know that on the 19th of November, 1991 a group of officers arrived in Negoslavci, officers from the security administration whose assignment was to select prisoners on the 18th -- on the 19th and 20th of November in Vukovar? Is something that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I have a general recollection that a group of security organ officers were arriving in the area, I assume, to carry out security organ-type functions, which would include screening of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pringle. Do you know that there was another team from the security section of the 1st Military District that arrived in the area with that same assignment, and they went about their work likewise on the 19th and 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't recall that, but it wouldn't surprise me because what was happening in Vukovar was a mass of prisoners of war, combatants, local forces, that had been engaged in operations, and therefore there would have been a heavy task to sort out combatants from civilians, et cetera. So it doesn't surprise me that these security organs are descending on the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at this time, the 18th and 19th, the 20th, the 21st, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, chief of the security administration, happened to be in the Vukovar area, came there several times, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, do you know that the Chief of Staff of the 1st Military District, General Vlado Stojanovic, issued an order that no POW exchanges were to be conducted without his prior consent?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me if you know that the negotiations on the surrender of the Mitnica group and the negotiations on the evacuation of the hospital were conducted by Colonel Pavkovic, deputy Chef de Cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I don't recall that in detail, but are you talking here about the higher-level negotiations that were either the outcome or resulted in the Zagreb agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pringle. Those negotiations were conducted by General Raseta. I'm talking about the negotiations conducted in Vukovar on the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, and the 20th.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the detail of those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, Mr. Pringle, that after the European monitors' team and the representatives of the Red Cross, after they came to the Vukovar Hospital and entered the Vukovar Hospital, were informed that a group of persons was taken away and that they had -- they did nothing to find out where those people were taken to and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I'm aware that the Zagreb agreement laid down the involvement of, amongst others, the International Red Cross, ECMM monitors, Medecins sans Frontieres, and perhaps others. I am also aware that they were held and delayed at a bridge approaching Vukovar, and I am aware that when they arrived at the hospital a certain element of the evacuation had already taken place. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you don't know about what I asked you about? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: If you're asking me, did I know that they did nothing to find out where those people were taken to and what happened to them, I don't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether they were told of the fact that people were taken away that same day. This is what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Did I know that they were informed that a group of persons was taken away. I'm not sure, but I think I recall that they were told that, and it probably would have been obvious to them, because they arrived in the middle, if I recall correctly, the evacuation operation. But I don't suppose they knew who had been taken away or how many or where to, because they, during, if I recall correctly, that time, were being delayed at the bridge trying to get into Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, although the term "command climate" that you speak about in your report did not exist as a term in the doctrine and regulations of the JNA in the way you presented, other than in the segments that you quoted, I must ask you whether you really believe that what happened at Ovcara was as a consequence of the command climate prevalent at the OG South command post, and in circumstances when we heard here that in Vukovar on site there were representatives of the strategic levels of command and control from the Ministry of Defence and the 1st Military District, with the task of coordinating and monitoring the situation and even participating in the negotiations, as we heard. Does this fact change your conclusions to a certain extent in relation to the command climate and do not all levels of command, from the strategic through the operational to the tactical level have an influence on the command climate, and not just an individual?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I addressed the subject of command climate in my report at some length between pages 13 and 18. And I acknowledge that the term command climate is not used in JNA doctrine, but what I'm talking about as command climate is readily recognised by JNA doctrine, and I reference a number of quotations to illustrate that. The command climate set by a commander at any level reflects his every act, his every action, his every utterance, his conduct, his behaviour, his views, his interpersonal relationships, the whole style of his command reflects the command climate. What you're, I think, trying to ask me, does the fact -- "I must ask you that whether you really believe that what happened at Ovcara was as a consequence of the command climate prevalent at the OG South command post." I can't comment on the command climate prevalent at the OG command -- OG South command post, because I was never there and I never saw it in action. But the way Colonel Mrksic commanded his forces, and the way he conducted himself, and the way he dealt with information flowing up and down the chain of command, in particular up the chain of command, and here I refer again to the report by Colonel -- his name's gone. 80 Motorised Brigade, concerning the events at Ovcara, the way he dealt with that sort of report does reflect the command climate that he is exuding about him. If you're asking me specifically, is what happened at Ovcara a direct result of the command climate, I can't answer that question. It's certainly a direct result of the actions taken or not taken by the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. You are now five minutes over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but the witness did not answer the question that I put to him. I asked him about the present strategic -- actually, members of the strategic command and what an effect that would have in the view of the witness, on the command climate in Vukovar in the time of the events at Ovcara, and he told us about everything else other than answering exactly what I asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: General, did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you give an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In that respect command climate is a permanent result of the way a commander acts. It is the tone and style he sets, it is what those subordinate to him believe is acceptable and non-acceptable to the commander, and in that respect the arrival of exterior organs into his area is not going to change the command climate he's already set, one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm Borivoje Borovic, and I represent Miroslav Radic. General, sir, were you present when the military expert, Mr. Theunens, testified in this case? Were you present from the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was sitting at the back over there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you drafted your report you had a list of witnesses from the Prosecution. My question is, since you said today that you read transcripts of three witnesses who testified here before the Trial Chamber, you also mentioned the names of the witnesses. Did you read any other transcripts, and would you be able to remember any names or you did not read any other transcripts other than those three?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I received at least two boxes of papers, and I concentrated on the three that I mentioned. There were others that I didn't have time to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean, General, that you did not read what witnesses P-002, P-022 stated in this trial? I'm thinking of the transcript and not of the statements provided to you by the Prosecutor. I am also thinking of the transcript of the testimony of Witness Vezmarovic, the testimony of Witness P-014. Does that mean that you did not read those transcripts of their testimony in this case, in this trial before you completed your report? I don't want to confuse you. The statements provided to you by the Prosecution and cited in your footnotes, yes, it's obvious that you read that. But I'm now talking about their testimony before this Trial Chamber. So could you please tell us that -- if you read that or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I find these questions very difficult, because I have read so much, and what I have been reading was really to see whether there was anything in the statements I was reading that led me to amend or change the opinions that I put in my report. I have to say that I didn't come across anything that led me to change my opinions in my report, but whether I read P-002, P-014 or a whole host of others, I'm sorry, I cannot recall unless I actually saw them and it would trigger my memory. That may not be very helpful, but it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I think that you were quite clear when you said that you didn't have time, that you read the transcript of the testimonies of all -- only those three witnesses that you considered as relevant.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I certainly read those three, and I dabbled in others, but what I was not necessarily taking into account who it was, but rather more what they were saying to see whether it should amend my view that I put in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the transcript of the testimony of the witness who was the commander of the military police company of the 80th Kragujevac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Can you give me his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Vezmarovic.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to finish with this question, did you read any kind of statement at any stage of drafting of your report by Witness Radoje Paunovic, the commander of the military police battalion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I'm just looking to see whether his name appears in the list of witness statements that I have got, and I don't think it does, unless he is hiding under a P number. Does he have a P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: General, he is on that list; there is no number that is used in relation to him. Do you recall this name, the first and last name, and did you come across that name? Did you also read the statement by Dr. Njavro?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do not have a Radoje Paunovic in the list of witness statements that I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Do you recall reading that statement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: As I say, it's not in the list of witness statements I was given, and therefore I will not have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And I still need to hear the answer in relation to Dr. Juraj Njavro, did you read his statement. He was employed at the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. He is Witness 43 in the list of witness statements. Whether I have footnoted him or not, I'm not sure, but I will have read -- I would have read his witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you would remember what he said if I were to ask you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's a dangerous assumption, but you can try me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I'm going to do that now, even though I wasn't planning to do that. This is a good challenge. Do you know if he mentioned Captain Radic and, if he did, in what context, because you say that you recollect the challenge -- actually, the statement. If it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I do remember that Captain Radic was mentioned in a number of statements as being present at the hospital. I have got --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: General, I'm talking about Njavro. Just Njavro. And then we will move on.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was in Njavro's statement or not, to be honest with you. But it was certainly in Witness P-030's statement, whoever P-030 is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So even though I did try, you did not recall what he said about Captain Radic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Let me just refer to what I've said about Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to confuse you, but it's true that you do not mention him anywhere in his footnote -- in your footnote, so I wouldn't have put this question to you had you not said, You can try me. You do not quote Dr. Njavro anywhere in your footnote, so I just wanted to be fair. I mean, if you remember anything that, all right; if not, then we will move on.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I think you've answered your own question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, continue.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have nothing further to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask the interpreters to use a method that we used earlier, when we talked about -- or when we used any military terms that relate in particular to my client, meaning that -- because we have a problem with the English language in relation to military terminology. Specifically I would like to ask the interpreters when I ask a question about komandir, to use the word komandir; when I'm talking about komandant, then I would like them to use the term komandant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please also follow the text on the screen. And this is why I actually mention this. Do you know the difference between a komandant and a komandir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I'm not really familiar with that, although I do recall it was being talked about -- you were asking the military expert, Mr. Theunens, the same question. I think they're different levels, but I'm -- the proper answer is -- is no. Just remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Officer commanding a company, would he be called a komandir, and would an officer commanding a battalion or a higher-level unit be called komandant on the basis of the regulations that you studied?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I believe that's the case, but if you wanted an absolutely certain answer, I would wish to go back to the regulation, for you to refer me to the proper text, and for me to say yes, there is it is in writing. But I believe that's what you were discussing with Mr. Theunens the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. This time I want to be absolutely proper in my conduct in relation to my learned friends from the Prosecution, and we disclosed documents last Friday, rules of service of company and platoon, and since obviously they did not have time to study that, today I am not going to discuss those documents. I am going to tender them through my own expert when the time comes, if the Trial Chamber permits. So I'm going to skip some of my questions precisely because I think that I questioned Mr. Theunens about that in detail, and before that Colonel Trifunovic gave precise, definite answers in interpreting these rules. Mr. Pringle, do you know at what level a staff is formed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Before I answer that question, I should say that I'm not here as an expert on JNA doctrine. That's not to say I have not read quite a lot of JNA doctrine, and I have not used it to draw conclusions on -- in my report on the generalities of command and control and behaviour. So I would just like to make that point. The expert in JNA doctrine you interviewed in the case of Mr. Theunens. In fact, I think you asked him exactly that question. Now, let me go back to your question. At what level -- I think it was at what level does a staff -- do staff happen. Well, you don't have a staff at a company level. You have a staff at battalion level, it's not very big, but you do have one. You have a much bigger staff at brigade level, and you have an even bigger staff at divisional or, in JNA terms, corps level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that you defined that. Based on the documents tendered here, and I think Mr. Theunens, to a large part reviewed most of those documents, if I were to tell you that the company commander, through orders and decisions of the battalion commander would be given the axis of attack and that higher-level units would be assigned areas of responsibility or areas of operation, would I be right as an amateur expert, when I say this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I believe battalion level or assault detachments were also given axes, because I think I've read a number of orders from OG South saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today we talked a little bit more about the climate command, and these are paragraphs 37 to 48 of your report. And mostly you link that term or concept with the komandant or the komandir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: No. The -- a command climate is a concept that you can apply to any level of command from the lowest, non-commissioned officer to the highest commissioned officer. It reflects the way they act, the way they conduct themselves, and the conclusions that those who they are in command of draw from their actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I absolutely agree with this conclusion of yours. In your report in paragraph 39, amongst others, you talk about the need for a personal authority, honesty, sincerity, discipline, good conduct, and other personal characteristics that you mention, courage and so on and so forth, moral responsibility as a particular characteristic. Am I right that these are some of the characteristics that an officer would need to have in order for the climate command to be at the desirable level?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, the point I'm making here, and what you've quoted, is footnote 58, drawn directly from JNA brigade rules, where, in effect, it's saying in different words, I mean let me read it: "Through his personal conduct where involvement in the interpretation of the SKJ policies ethical standing, courage, ability, fairness, cool-headedness, consistency, and respect for the personality and opinion of subordinates, the commander vitally influences the entire condition of the brigade," because this is brigade rules, "... of the brigade, especially the morale of units and command." But exactly those character traits would apply at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, witnesses P-022, P-002, Witness Trifunovic and most witnesses I have questioned about the circumstances in relation to Captain Radic, and the reference for P-022 is page 5083-15, and for P-002, this is 10555-5. In relation to Captain Radic, they all emphasise the following features: Brave, courageous officer, he was with his soldiers at the front, he was honest, he was disciplined. An example was given that was discussed here at trial of 40 volunteers who had violated the rules of discipline. Radic had them disarmed and forced them to leave the front. He marched them away from the front line. Are you familiar with this information? Are you familiar with any of these statements that were previously given, not taking into the account the transcripts from this trial?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the statements you've quoted there, no. I have no reason to disbelieve them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have much time, and I don't think it will be a good idea for me to go into everything that was actually said. We tendered into evidence a number of newspaper pieces. They all emphasise Radic's bravery and so on and so forth. If you take this to be true, if you take to be true what a number of witnesses stated, and it is on the record, would that not mean that at company level, which is where Captain Radic's was, there simply had to be the sort of command climate that you describe as necessary and desirable, given these assumptions, of course.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't necessarily agree that. I have no reason not to believe that Captain Radic was an extremely brave officer and had performed in such a manner. But that, in itself, is not sufficient to create the totality of the command climate that I'm referring to. And let me give you two examples. If I recall correctly, Captain Radic's headquarters was close by, if not co-located with the local TO and volunteer forces headquarters and so he was intimately knowledgeable of how they behaved, and yet when he was informed that -- of the events at Ovcara --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My apologies, sir. May I interrupt for a second? You are talking about things that we are about to get to, but at a later stage. Just to be fair, can you keep -- can you please keep this until later. You can perhaps draw these conclusions when we get to that stage. If I am hearing you correctly, you keep using the term Captain Radic's headquarters. I'm not sure if the interpretation is correct. Are you perhaps referring to his command post, although that, strictly speaking, would not be accurate either?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Now, I think you would call it an observation post, which to me is something completely different. Yes, okay. Let me strict -- stay strictly within the confines of your question. Is the fact that Captain Radic has a reputation as an extremely brave officer, does that mean that he has all the attributes for a correct command climate as I've described it. Answer, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That was not my question. Bravery is just one feature that was required, but I've enumerated all the others. Honesty, discipline, I've given you that example about him sending those people packing, because they had breached discipline, rules of discipline. I talked about all the protected witnesses at this trial, OTP witnesses who could not but admit that he was the most honourable and bravest officer there, that he treated people well. These are different questions that I asked a wide range of witnesses. Bearing in mind precisely the qualities that you list in your report as being desirable or necessary for an officer, whether this was a command post or indeed whether Captain Radic had effective control, or actual control, is something that we will be getting to. My question is: In your interpretation of the principles of command and control, which is what you do in your report, after all, you did not specify the command and control relationship at komandir level and komandant level. And in terms of the doctrine that was applied, these were by no means identical. However, if this distinction between komandir and komandant is a problem for you, and if you believe that this was covered by Mr. Theunens before you, please by no means consider yourself compelled to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have no difficulty distinguishing between the roles and responsibilities of komandir and komandant, if one is loosely put at company level and the other is loosely put at battalion or assault detachment level. That does not, in any way, reflect different requirements in terms of setting a proper command climate. Exactly the same criteria would be required as indeed it would be to the komandir's subordinates in their own right. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's leave it at that. My next question: In your report, you say that on the 19th or 20th of November Captain Radic was at the hospital as a private individual. Is that right, sir? This is in your report, paragraph 84.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That is in my --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That indeed what it says, that's my first question.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: You're asking me to refer to a bit in my report that has been underlined, because it was drawn from a witness statement by Borivoje Tesic, under which I understand there is a problem. But if you'd like me to read that out, I will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The footnote is underlined.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: The footnote, 126 and 7 are underlined. What I said in my report: "As it is apparent that Captain Miroslav Radic was present at the hospital during the evacuation on 19th and 20th November without any apparent orders and apparently not in command of his own assault detachment troops, he appears to be have been present in an individual capacity." Now, that was a conclusion I drew from what I had read. It did not appear that he was there in command of his own company. But he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you only base this on the statement that is underlined in red, which probably means that we can't use it, or is there another piece of evidence that leads you to that same conclusion; namely, that Radic was there in his own private capacity?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That Radic was there appears in a statement by Witness P-030.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But being there in a private capacity is not something that we can really derive from your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, no, the statement "in a private capacity" is the conclusion I drew, because I did not gain the impression in the reports and statements that I was reading that Captain Radic was there commanding his own troops. He had just happened to be there, apparently, working with Major Sljivancanin, and he was, as I say in my report, therefore witness to ill-treatment of evacuees by TO and volunteers. That's -- that's the point I was making.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us assume for a moment that he was there in a private capacity, and let us assume for a moment that the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion, Borivoje Tesic was there too, at the same time as Radic, on the 19th of November. Could he, in the presence of his superior officer, possibly ever be there in purely private capacity?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I can't comment on that, because I -- it is not apparent to me why he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Under the rules, when an officer of a lower rank happens to be in the same place as his superior officer, who also happens to hold a higher rank, how do you imagine the lower-ranking officer could be there in a private capacity under any set of rules known to us, or would one prefer to assume that he was there under the command of his superior officer and for that reason only?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I think when I say "private capacity," I'm really referring to the fact that as far as I could make out from what I read he was not in command of his own troops there. Now, that does not mean that he could not have been there in a reconnaissance capacity, a liaison capacity, or any other capacity. But the fact is, I simply don't know why he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 19th and 20th of November, 1991, do you know what a JNA officer's uniform looked like and could you describe it for us, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Not really. But sort of spider camouflage, I believe. Side hat or steel helmet. The answer is I cannot give you the detail of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While studying this case, have you ever come across the fact that anyone at all in the infantry companies was wearing blue or green berets? What I'm putting to you is that this was not standard issue in the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I don't believe I've read anything that has stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, on the 20th of November do you know who was providing security at the Vukovar Hospital on the 20th of November? Which specific unit?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I believe, and here again I'm recalling from memory, that it was elements of a motorised battalion of -- and I'm not sure whether it was Guards Motorised Brigade or 80th Motorised Brigade, but I also believe from the many statements that I read that on the 20th of November the person in charge or taking charge of the operation at the hospital appeared to be Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question was if you knew who was physically securing the hospital. You studied a great deal of documents. Which military unit could that have been? Who could have been in charge of providing that sort of security for that particular sort of facility?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That is a duty that could fall naturally to elements of a motorised battalion or, equally well, to elements of a military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who is authorised to frisk people, members of just which unit? Do you know who was doing the frisking, who was sending the people to the buses that were there following the frisking? Have you come across this sort of information, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I did read statements about what was going on at the hospital. Who was actually doing the frisking I'm not sure I can recall, but that is a duty that would fall naturally to military police and/or security organs. If by "frisking" you mean searching and sorting out and screening of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Company, Miroslav Radic, even if he had been there, could he possibly have exercised command, or indeed issued any orders to the military police company that was there or indeed any military police officers who may have happened to be there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, it depends under what circumstances he was there. If he had been authorised to be there in some capacity, official capacity, shall we say hypothetically as the assistant to Major Sljivancanin, for example, then he may well have been authorised to give orders on Major Sljivancanin's behalf if Major Sljivancanin himself had been authorised to take control of the operation. It's a hypothetical answer to a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My last question. If he was there in a private capacity, as you say, all the more then he would certainly have not been in a position to issue any orders, would he?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I say again, when I talk about private capacity, I was meaning that it was not apparent to me that his own company troops were there under his command. Whether he would have been in a position to issue any orders would have resulted directly from the reason and -- and authorisation which resulted in his being there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You don't know the reasons, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have said many times I have not -- I am not aware of the reason why Radic was there when his troops were not. But it is -- it is plain that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It is not plain that he was there. However, we are now ready to call it a day, I believe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: In the statements that I have read, it is incontrovertible that he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we can challenge that very efficiently tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, that's for another day, not for today. We resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, finish by 1.45 in the day. So thank you very much. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 23rd day of June, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
